It’s tomorrow for you. What’s going to happen tomorrow?
It’s tonight. It’s a great day here. It looks beautiful. It looks like it’s going to be an amazing day.

At this point in the AI news cycle, I feel like I can just demand to know what’s going to happen tomorrow, and everyone understands the urgency behind that question. There’s a lot going on with Atlassian. There’s a lot going on with your products. There’s a lot going on in the very concept of SaaS businesses and business processes generally.
Let’s start at the very start. I think people know Atlassian. They know Jira. I started my career as a Trello person. Tell people what you think Atlassian is today.

Atlassian is a platform that enables businesses to collaborate and manage work across their teams. We connect their business teams and their technology teams to handle the most challenging work problems in a singular platform across any organization that is technologically driven.

For any organization that has software and technology as its core competitive advantage, we make a broad platform that allows them to collaborate on content, manage projects, and unleash the knowledge of their teams and organizations across their business, their strategy, operations, all the way through to their service teams in all areas of their business. It’s a very large platform now that we provide.

Just in terms of what work is today and what it might be in the future as we add more and more AI to these enterprises, maybe this is too reductive, but I have always thought of Atlassian as a company that makes tools to help teams figure out what they’re going to do tomorrow. Jira is a perfect example of this. You don’t do the software engineering in Jira, but Jira helps you organize large teams of software engineers and file tickets and prioritize problems and tasks.

I was a Trello person a long time ago. My goal in life now is to never use any enterprise software. I feel like that’s a sign of true success if you’re just an iPad person in first class. I’m working on it. I’m not saying I’m there yet, but that’s one of my goals.

But there was a time when I was the managing editor of The Verge and my job, straightforwardly, was to look at Trello every day and make sure everyone was doing the right thing at the right time. And I’ve always thought of Atlassian as that class of products. We’re going to organize the processes of the company.
There’s something about AI that’s changing that. Has that conception of Atlassian changed for you? Is it changing faster because of AI?

Understanding what work you have to do at an individual level like Trello, at a team level like Jira, or at an organizational level like our Strategy Collection for large-scale strategy and operations — that is definitely a big part of what we do.

Understanding where processes are at — It’s less about work to do than processes. If you think about a business as a system of processes that are put together, everything in a business is some sort of system. It’s a process in the collection of all these, and how well we execute them is what your business is doing. The fundamentals of that haven’t changed. The way those processes run, the number of them running, and how to figure out what’s going on hasn’t changed.

We think about Jira as a human reference to work. When we say that, it’s a really interesting term because, as you said, the work is not done in Jira. Developers don’t live in Jira. Marketers don’t live in Jira. Finance people don’t live in Jira. Jira is a workflow engine with highly collaborative parts that enables teams to understand what they, their colleagues, and their broader organization are doing. That’s why agents and AI and other things are going to increase the speed of those processes. In a lot of ways, they will increase the reliability, the quality, and the consistency of output of certain processes.

They also put more emphasis on where the humans, the judgment, the intuition, the human bits that are unique, and the initiation come from. It’s our job to make sure that that’s all still understandable so someone can just look at any level of their business and know what the fuck’s going on. What are people doing? Are we successfully doing whatever it is that we’re trying to do, whether that’s service function in a finance sales deal, exception service desk to work out how many exceptions did we give out in sales this quarter, or it’s an engineering team who’s trying to work out, “There’s stuff happening all over the place. What did we build this month? Or what are we going to build next month?” All of those things are incredibly hard to do at scale and volume in a business.

One of the more important features of the tools you’ve built is legibility. It’s user experience. You have a big database of exceptions given out by salespeople, and you need to look at a dashboard and see how the company’s doing. Or you have a whole bunch of tasks, and Jira will let you see at various different levels of abstraction how many tasks are being completed at any given time.

That was something that was very important for human managers. A lot of the capability unlock of businesses as they added software like the software Atlassian makes is to just be able to see and coordinate more things at a higher scale.

The turn that’s coming is that maybe those databases aren’t going to be looked at by human beings anymore, or they’re going to be fed into more synthesized databases, or AI is going to make some other kind of information at different levels of abstraction. I know you’ve got a product called Rovo which feels like the new face of Atlassian in some ways.
What’s the path here? What does the end state look like?

There’s no doubt AI is going to help with a lot of those processes. There’s no doubt it’s going to pick up some steps in a process. Most businesses at the moment have a process, and they’re using AI to automate 80% of this step. It may not be 80% of the distance. It can be the width. If you think about that sales deal exception process that you just mentioned again there, if AI can take 80% of the exception — say this customer wants 45 days, not 30 days — and we can write a relatively readable document, AI is pretty good at reading the document and saying, “Yep, this one’s fine.”

But there’s going to be a customer that needs a lot more complex exceptions. They say, “I want to pay in 90 days in this way, and I want this thing and that thing.” That needs to go to a human for intuition and judgment. So 80% of those may be easier done with AI now because it’s very capable at processing our rules in this particular part of our business, and that’s great. It’ll increase the speed of the process, the quality of it.

It doesn’t take away the need to know what’s going on. Someone in the business will still need to know, “How many exceptions did we give?” What happens in most of these areas is businesses find way more ways to make themselves scale and efficient, and they find way more ways to make higher-quality products and services with AI. I see this all the time where they are utilizing AI in ways that people don’t expect. It’s not all about mechanistic efficiency. There’s a huge amount of quality that is able to be measured and understood that was never before. The deal exception process is a good example because it’s actually a very human process. It’s not usually rule-driven. The rule-driven parts are easy. It’s the non-rule-driven parts that are more complicated and require judgment.

The business still needs to know, for that process, “Do we need to add more people to this process? Do we need to change it? How much is going through it?” You still have a lot of work to understand the flow of work around an enterprise, which gets more complicated as the flow’s volume goes up a lot.

I’m asking because I’m headed towards a series of questions about the supposed SaaSpocalypse, and I’m very curious where you think tool providers like Atlassian fit next to the frontier models are just going to eat more and more capability. Eventually, Claude will just do this for you. You’ll say to Claude, “Run my business for me.” In the backend, Claude will burn a bunch of tokens, and it’ll just do it all for you, which is a promise that many, many people seem to believe in.

You’re describing a somewhat different path where the tools get smarter or more capable because of AI, and you’re still adding a lot of human judgment, but at no point is a frontier model just coming and running your entire business for you.

If a frontier model is capable of coming and running the entire business for you, if it’s truly running the whole thing, even assuming four or five years worth of increase, you have a relatively simple business. Most businesses aren’t simple. They are global conglomerations of rules, compliance, laws, staff in different places, human inconsistency — which is the same as saying human creativity — that they’re putting it all together to try to deliver products and services for their customers in their industry: healthcare, university, finance, automotive, or whatever the industry is.

They’re trying to compete with some other business. They are still going to have a huge number of humans, I would argue more knowledge workers, more developers, in five to 10 years time than today because the ability to do tasks to compete will go up.

The bar for competition will go up in almost all these industries. You will still have a huge amount of things to go do. Most of the things that we think are simple will get done for you. That is the history of technology. I’m a big fan of saying AI is just technology. What we can do with spreadsheets, what we can do with the internet, what we can do with ordering goods online… You think, “Once Amazon arrives, we’ll all just never have to go to the shops again.” It doesn’t happen.

I heard someone talking about bank branches as an analogy, which I thought was a really good one. Around 2000 when mobile banking came along, everyone thought bank branches were dead. Bank branches started closing down. Everyone wasn’t going to go to their branch anymore. It was a pretty negative place. At least it was in Australia. I’m pretty sure it was in America as well.

If you look over the last 10 years, bank branches are increasing. People are like, “Huh, this is a narrative violation. Why is this?” And the answer is bank branches did close down. People did go to internet banking. They did use their mobile app. They don’t go into the branch anymore with a passport to say, “I’d like to send $100 to Nilay, please. Here are his details,” and write them all down.

But bank branches have adapted. The reason they’re growing is there is a huge customer service element to a bank branch. The services they provide today are totally different than what they provided 25 years ago due to the technology of the bank and the availability of things. They are much more about helping you with higher-level processes and services than they ever have been.

That turns out to be, presumably, profitable for the banks, which is why they’re opening new branches. Bank branches are going up. The things those branches are doing are totally different to what they were 25 years ago. I think you’ll see the same thing with knowledge workers and everything else, that it will still be incredibly important.
I don’t see that part changing.

I am working my way up to getting Jamie Dimon on the show to find out what happens in all the Chase Bank branches in New York, because I don’t actually know, but we’ll set that aside. Jamie will come on the show. We’ll ask, and we’ll figure it out.

One of the reasons I’m asking all these foundational existential questions is to understand how you feel about Atlassian’s relationship to businesses and how businesses might change as we add new technology. I agree with your general framing that automation technology arriving to a business is a pretty familiar phenomenon, but there’s something else going on with AI that is either making that faster or more dramatic. It’s obviously happening to your business as well. You’re the CEO of Atlassian, and you’ve made some changes around AI.
I want to ask you the Decoder questions now. How many people is Atlassian today? And how is it structured?

We are, I think publicly, 12,000-13,000-odd people around the world. We are structured globally, I would say. We are “Team Anywhere.” Employees have the choice to come into an office or not. About 60 percent of people come in three days a week or more. About 25 percent of people don’t come in a single day per week. We run as a globally distributed company as we have done since the start. When you start in Australia and San Francisco, you kind of get used to the Pacific Ocean being a little bit of a distribution. This was before Zoom. We used to have these giant Polycom systems in meeting rooms. We don’t have those anymore. Technological progress is nice.

We have customers all around the world. We have staff all around the world. We are structured functionally, I guess you would say, with a lot of matrices internally. I don’t know if that’s the answer you’re looking for.
No, that’s absolutely the answer I’m looking for. What do you mean by “functionally with a lot of matrices”?

We have a CRO. We have a CFO. We have two CTOs at the moment. We have two large product groups, each of which has a CTO and a chief product officer, one in the enterprise and emerging side and one in the future of teamwork side.

Our products are organized into collections. We have collections of apps that are all built on a single platform. Well over half of our R&D is on the platform. The apps are increasingly a smaller amount of the proportional total investment in building. More and more is on the singular Atlassian platform. Customers hire us as a platform across their business to get work done, not for a single application.

That requires a matrix internally. We don’t have salespeople per product, if you want to think about it that way. The sales, customer success, and the FDEs are all customer-related motions. They’re organized as per the customers and their geographies and their size and scale. Then we obviously have to have designers and product managers on particular products who care about the purpose of a product, so you end up instantly with the matrix between how the customers are organized and how the products are organized.

We have a giant platform. We have the technical platform that runs across all the products. It’s a very large platform team. We then have finance and talent and other things that are also broad processes. Naturally, you end up with collaborative areas that you have to get together, and we manage that through our operating processes.
Do you use the Atlassian platform to run Atlassian?

We do. We run entirely on the Atlassian platform. I used to say we’re the number one user — we’re not anymore — of our strategy and operations products to understand what our business is focusing on, what our large-scale goals are, how the people, the investments, and the technical systems all come together, and what is going right and wrong across all of those. We are a big believer in our Strategy Collection to operate a large-scale business.
One of my favorite questions to ask enterprise software CEOs is how much they personally use the enterprise software. How much do you personally use your products?
An awful lot.
What’s your number one feature request for your teams?

My number one feature request is usually continual UI congruence. I guess that’s the category that people would put it in. I’m a bit of a stickler for design and consistency. We want to achieve eventual consistency in design, in which we’ve come a huge distance in the last five years. In the last two years, we’ve been truly world-class at doing it. That’s usually my biggest area where I use a lot of our products on a regular basis. As such, I’m moving around the platform, and I’m looking for ways where this thing over here happens this way. They do it better over there. We’re trying to achieve that eventual consistency across a large product surface area.

I use Dia, our web browser. I think 96 to 97 percent of Atlassian now uses Dia on a regular basis. I mean, that’s a daily basis, so I literally spend many, many, many hours of the day on it. We are building a web browser for ourselves because we’ve reached the point that we feel, “This thing should just be better for knowledge workers.” We’ve already built, I would argue, the best browser for knowledge workers in the world, and it’s getting much, much, much better. Keep watching this space.
So, yes, I would say there’s no 24-hour period that goes by where I don’t use one of our products. I doubt there’s a six-hour period that goes by where I don’t use one of our products at the moment.
I want to talk about Dia in a second, because I’m very curious about that acquisition. Obviously, we covered The Browser Company very deeply at The Verge. That was a big acquisition for you guys.

Setting that aside for just one second, one of the things I’m particularly curious about here is the distinction between the platform and the products that run on the platform. Again, maybe this is just reductive, but it sounds like there’s a big layer of capability, and the products are expressions of those capabilities in different ways, but they’re all running on the same core platform.
Is that how you think about it?
cb89e8735c469d5a: PETALING JAYA: The Kedah veterinary services department (JPVK) has reminded the public not to take matters into their own hands by killing animals suspected of being infected with rabies.
Its health division head, Dr Ummi Sumilah Soraya Johar, urged the public not to catch, hit or kill animals, particularly stray dogs, roaming in their communities.
She said members of the public should instead immediately report them to the authorities for further action, Bernama reported.
Following the rabies case detected in Kubang Pasu, JPVK has opened two operations room, one in Alor Setar that can be contacted at 04-7025336, and another in Kubang Pasu at 04-9162207.
She appeared on the Kedah state health department's Facebook Live platform today to talk on rabies.
A 31-year-old man died in Kubang Pasu yesterday after being bitten by a stray dog in August.
Ummi advised the public against handling sick animals due to the high risk of infection through contact with saliva or blood, or bites, even if the wound was small.
She said rabies was usually transmitted by dogs, although other mammals such as cats, bats and cattle could also carry the disease.
“In animals, particularly dogs, symptoms can appear as early as seven to 14 days after infection.
“There is usually excessive salivation. When the nervous system is affected, the dog's jaw may droop and its behaviour may change.
“A previously docile dog may become aggressive or start biting without provocation, while unusual barking may also indicate that its nervous system has been affected.”
Ummi advised dog owners to immediately get their pets vaccinated against rabies if they had not already done so.

Kedah public health medicine specialist Dr Tan Wei Leong advised those bitten or scratched by animals, whether dogs or cats, to immediately wash the wound with soap under running water for at least 15 minutes to reduce infection.
“Never delay treatment or assume that a small wound is harmless.
“Rabies is a viral disease that attacks the nervous system, including the brain, and can be fatal once symptoms appear.”
He said the risk of death could be reduced through immediate preventive treatment after a bite, including receiving rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).
He said those who had previously received rabies vaccinations and subsequently sustained a new bite must still seek immediate medical treatment and assessment from a doctor.
He clarified that tetanus injections and antibiotics, which are commonly administered after a person is bitten by an animal, were not the same as PEP.

Hosts Japan are a distant second in the medals table and South Korea third.

Sri Lanka play Nepal and Bangladesh face Malaysia in the last two quarter-finals on Tuesday.
However, more rain is forecast.

Golf is due to start Wednesday but the wet weather ruined practice.
'Totally unfair'

Pakistan's group game with Uzbekistan had to be pushed back 45 minutes.
"This is another mismanagement by Japan at the ongoing Asian Games," Pakistan captain Murad Jehan said from the bus in an Instagram video.

"We have a very important game and the bus driver does not know in which gymnasium we are going to play," he said in the clip, with a caption reading, "Embarrassing situation at Japan Asian Games 2026. Totally unfair," he added.
He added: "We couldn't expect this in Japan. There is a lot of mismanagement".
It is more embarrassing for the red-faced organisers of the Games, where there have been numerous complaints about the accommodation and transport services.

97a58c093e76aac1: OpenAI agents apparently spent two months hammering a United Nations (UN) data API, trying increasingly creative ways to bypass the barriers they encountered. Researcher Rowan H-J uncovered the activity by analyzing roughly 16,500 scans of the UN Conference on Trade and Development's UNCTADstat API recorded between April 13 and June 19, 2026. Rowan claims it’s "highly likely" the traffic came from OpenAI agents, based on links to previously documented OpenAI "wiki swarms," overlapping Azure IP addresses, and payloads carrying labels including “CHATGPTTEST1” and “OAI_META_1312.” OpenAI told The Register it is looking into the findings, though it stopped short of explicitly confirming that its agents were responsible for the activity Rowan documented. "We're aware of reports of OpenAI models accessing publicly available information from the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development's Data Hub," an OpenAI spokesperson told us. "We're reviewing these findings and have reached out to the UN to offer a briefing with the team conducting that review." The spokesperson pointed to OpenAI's previously announced review of what it calls "misaligned model activity," saying most of the behavior examined so far involved routine research, including accessing public websites to answer questions. "Some involved government websites because our models often turn to them as authoritative sources of public information," the spokesperson added. Assuming the researcher is right, the interesting part isn't that AI agents wanted to get their synthetic mitts on some UN statistics. It's what happened when they couldn't. The agents appear to have been hunting for fairly unexciting public data on things like trade, employment, and productive capacity. But requests to UNCTADstat didn't always work the way they wanted, and instead of admitting defeat, they kept trying different routes. According to Rowan's analysis, the agents experimented with third-party services that could make requests on their behalf and built bits of JavaScript to fetch the data. One of the more unusual detours involved Google's XSS training game, a deliberately vulnerable site for learning about cross-site scripting. The agents appear to have put it to rather more practical use, using it to host JavaScript that made requests to UNCTADstat. On June 1, one attempt returned nine rows of employment data. The agents also stumbled across a trick that appeared to get around UNCTADstat refusing a particular type of request. After the straightforward approach failed, they altered the address using double URL encoding. This time the server returned a successful response. Rowan counted the same technique being used 55 times between May 4 and June 19. There was plenty of flailing around in between. The agents repeatedly guessed different names for the API key parameter, tried different ways to construct requests, and apparently tried to dodge a filter that may not even have existed. The API key itself wasn't some crown jewel pilfered from a UN server. Rowan notes that UNCTADstat's own data viewer sends the same key from users' browsers. What stands out is how persistent the agents appear to have been set to be. When one route failed, they tried another, bringing in third-party services and changing how requests were made until they got the data they were after. Which, of course, is what we're told makes AI agents useful: give them a goal and let them figure out the steps required to achieve it. Things get a little more interesting when one of those steps involves working out how to get past somebody else's technical restrictions. Or, possibly, some might infer, not being told to obey guardrails. Why the agents were doing any of this remains unclear. Rowan doesn’t have the prompts they were given and suggests the pattern could fit an internal OpenAI question set used for training or evaluation. There are other breadcrumbs pointing toward OpenAI. Shortly after some of the UNCTADstat activity, an account called “PublicDataResearchAgentT93214” created a page on FractalWiki containing the same API URLs. Rowan also found that 45 of the 54 Azure IP addresses associated with UNCTAD-related activity on the wikis had previously edited DseWiki during the earlier agent swarm. All that ingenuity for some UN statistics. Imagine what happens when the prize is a little more interesting. ®
36120f54827a98b0: METZ: Pope Leo XIV warned on Monday that relations between nations were becoming increasingly uncivilised, with people boasting of "lies and deceit", urging Europe to help break the cycle and foster respect in international ties.
Speaking in the city of Metz near the border with Germany, where he was wrapping up a four-day visit to France, Leo did not mention any world leaders by name.
The pope sees Europe as a counterweight to major powers and has in the past called on the EU to overcome tensions and rediscover unity in pursuit of peace in Ukraine and beyond.
Leo, the first US pontiff, has repeatedly clashed with president Donald Trump in recent months over the harsh crackdown on immigration in the US and the war on Iran.
Trump has called him "weak" on crime and "terrible" on foreign policy.

"Relations between individuals and states are becoming increasingly uncivilised. The value of keeping one's word is dismissed. Instead, people boast of lies and deceit," the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics said, alongside French president Emmanuel Macron.
"Europe can help to break this cycle through the respect for others that it has learned to cultivate and preserve," Leo said, on the first official papal visit to France in nearly two decades.
Throughout his trip, the pope has appeared smiling and warm, readily engaging with crowds.

On Monday morning, the pontiff, who is passionate about aviation, spent half an hour in the cockpit of the Air France plane that flew him to the city on the final leg of the apostolic journey, Air France told AFP.
'Force for peace'
Metz is closely associated with Robert Schuman, considered one of the founding fathers of the EU, who is buried just outside the city.

In his speech on unity in Europe, Leo also urged "courage in negotiation" and compromise to put an end to war on the continent, in an apparent reference to Russia's war against Ukraine, now in its fifth year and showing no sign of abating.
"Today, sadly, war has returned, even to Europe: a new 'senseless slaughter,' claiming countless civilian lives every day," he said.
"We need to commit ourselves to patient dialogue, to show courage in negotiation and to be willing to give up some positions for the greater good of peace," the pontiff added.
Leo appealed for unity as nationalist movements are gaining strength in Europe.
France's anti-immigration far right hopes to win next year's election and succeed Macron, a centrist.
The pontiff said Europe was "entering a new stage" with the arrival of men and women fleeing war and persecution, urging countries to welcome and integrate them.

"We must grasp the historical significance of what is taking place, namely an unprecedented encounter between peoples and cultures, which calls us to rediscover our roots in new and creative ways, while at the same time listening carefully to others," he said.
Macron, for his part said Europe should counter resurgent nationalism.
Europe "must rediscover the courage of its founders - yes, courage - in order to become the force for peace, independence, and democracy that it is meant to be," he said.
"The courage not to give in to withdrawal, to hatred of others, to the return of nationalisms that divide," he said.
'Something has changed'
Leo has repeatedly called for peace, a message shaped in part by his family history.
His father, Louis Marius Prevost, who served in the US Navy, witnessed war firsthand, taking part in the D-Day landings in Normandy on June 6, 1944.
In Metz, home to around 120,000 people, the pope's visit had sparked excitement, with hotels fully booked and restaurants reporting a surge in reservations.
"This is his fourth day in France, and you can feel that something has changed in the atmosphere," said Florence Prieur, 45.
"We're seeing more kindness and more joy," Prieur said.
Philippe Ballot, archbishop of Metz, said the visit carried strong symbolic significance in a city shaped by "three wars, including two world wars".
8e9276fd303ebd10: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 28 — While most people are fast asleep, thousands of packets of rice and side dishes, as well as kuih — all traditional delicacies of Kelantan — are transported hundreds of kilometres from the east coast almost daily to reach customers in the Klang Valley, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka.
One of the businesses driving this delivery chain is Nasi Berlauk Kelate Express (NBK Express), operated by Mohd Syafrini Azmi, 38.

Embarking on the venture a decade ago, his delivery service started with about 200 packets per trip before expanding to more than 3,000 packets for each trip to the Klang Valley. The company has also since opened delivery routes to Terengganu and Pahang.

Speaking to Bernama recently about the business, Mohd Syafrini said it was his friend Mohd Yusri Mohd Yusoff, 38, who came up with the idea of bringing Kelantanese food to markets outside the state due to the sizeable Kelantanese community in the Klang Valley and beyond.

“When I first started, I used a Myvi car and at one point rented an Avanza. But as the orders grew, the cars could no longer accommodate the orders, while the food could also be damaged when the packets were stacked on top of one another.
“So, I switched to vans (one each for the Klang Valley route and Terengganu/Pahang route) and have continued using them to this day,” he said.

Mohd Syafrini said initially, he was only delivering nasi berlauk Air Dingin, but the “menu” has since expanded to a wider variety of Kelantan specialities, including rice with chicken, fish and beef dishes from popular “brands” such as Kak Chik, Tengku Noor, Depey Tanggo and Kakak Aisyah, as well as Nasi Kerabu Paloh.
His company also transports a variety of traditional Kelantanese kuih and delicacies, including tepung bungkus, lompat tikam, nasi tumpang, ketupat and nasi kapit sambal.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

One of the businesses driving this delivery chain is Nasi Berlauk Kelate Express (NBK Express), which started on a small scale in 2015 by delivering food from Tumpat to Gua Musang. It now sends more than 3,000 packets on each trip to the Klang Valley, while also operating new routes to Terengganu and Pahang. — Bernama pic

He said more than 20 suppliers and food operators in Kelantan are now supplying the various dishes and delicacies to NBK Express, with collection taking place at several locations in the state, including Tumpat, Wakaf Che Yeh and Machang.

For the Klang Valley route, the van stops in Gombak, Selangor, where the food packets are handed over to over 80 agents and runners who distribute them to restaurants and other sellers in the Klang Valley, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka.

NBK Express opened the new route to Terengganu and Pahang two months ago, transporting about 2,000 packets of food on each trip to several areas, including Setiu, Kuala Terengganu, Paka, Kuantan and Rompin.
Mohd Syafrini, who resides in Selangor, said for the Klang Valley route, the driver begins collecting supplies in Tumpat at around 10 pm before heading to other collection points.
“The van usually leaves for Kuala Lumpur at around 11pm.

“After about five hours on the road, the van can arrive in Gombak as early as 4am, where the food is collected by agents and runners for distribution in their respective areas,” he said, adding that punctuality is crucial as some agents start selling as early as 6.30am to meet demand from customers heading to work.
However, sometimes the van driver is unable to reach the destination on time due to incidents such as accidents, vehicle breakdowns and punctured tyres.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A Nasi Berlauk Kelate Express (NBK) food runner collects food and traditional ‘kuih’ from Kelantan after they arrive in the Klang Valley. — Bernama pic
“In 2017, the van skidded on the highway near Lipis, Pahang, due to slippery road conditions before spinning and overturning, leaving the vehicle completely wrecked.

“When we found out about it, the first thing that came to mind was the driver’s safety. Fortunately, he was safe, but the company had to bear the cost of the food (that could not be supplied that day) and refund payments to the agents,” he said.

For Mohd Syafrini, the most meaningful aspect of running the business is that it has created income opportunities for food operators in Kelantan as well as sellers across the Klang Valley and other states.

“For me, the satisfaction does not come from my achievement alone because, indirectly, this effort also provides a source of income for others,” he said, adding that he is also considering expanding his delivery service to Johor if time and logistical constraints can be overcome.

Meanwhile, Datuk Azri Che Zan, who operates Stesen Bukuh restaurant in Puchong, Selangor, said he has been selling the Kelantan food packets supplied by NBK Express since September 12, after seeing strong demand for the food in several other areas, including Shah Alam and Bangi.
“We did not expect such an encouraging response. Our highest sales reached about 2,000 packets on September 16, which sold out within just three hours, starting from 7am,” he said.

He said the majority of customers were Kelantanese who said the taste was close to what they enjoyed in their home state, with nasi kapit sambal and Kak Chik dishes among the most popular choices. — Bernama
e45615181881c9f6: NAGOYA, Sept 28 — Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Carlos Alcaraz are all obsessed with it, and yesterday the fast-growing racquet sport of padel made its Asian Games debut with officials hoping a place at the Olympics is getting closer.
Padel, a cross between tennis and squash on courts surrounded by glass walls, is played by an estimated 38 million people and has ambitions to become a major global sport.
It took another step towards that goal at the Asian Games in Nagoya after being added to the continent’s biggest sporting spectacular as a medal event.

After winning her opening match with doubles partner Danna Abad, Philippines player Joshea Malazarte told AFP: “Padel in Europe is really big and it has just started here, so we’re just glad that they added padel.”
Padel originated in Latin America and has exploded in popularity in the last decade, notably in Europe.
Officials say the sport is played in 170 countries and territories, with 85,000 courts around the globe.
It is still relatively unknown in Games host Japan, and there was curiosity among some of the crowd at the modest Higashi Sports Centre.
Tickets for the event were free, and one spectator told AFP that she and her friend had dropped in to take a look before heading off for lunch.
Another, 60-year-old Yuko Hiraiwa, said she enjoyed the action but thought the crowd was “a bit quiet”.
“I play padel but this was the first time I’ve seen it live,” she said.
“It was really dynamic and exciting.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Lebanon’s Tamim El Hallak and Ralph Tohme (front) serve against Japan’s Teruaki Ando and Shinnosuke Nakamura during the men’s pairs padel first round match at the Nagoya City Highashi Sports Center in Nagoya September 28, 2026. — AFP pic
Smash hit
The sedate atmosphere in Nagoya was a far cry from padel’s popularity in other parts of the world.
The sport has a professional tour circuit and an event held at the Roland Garros tennis stadium in Paris this month attracted over 80,000 people.
A galaxy of padel-playing sports stars including football icons Ronaldo and Messi and Formula One driver Max Verstappen have also given it a boost.
Padel has already appeared at the European Games, and International Padel Federation (IPF) official Donatella Del Gaudio said the next goal is the Olympics.
“We are working hard to make it happen soon,” she said.
“We just need to be patient, diligent and respect the Olympic timeline.”
Padel is usually played as a doubles game and uses solid rather than stringed racquets.
The courts are much smaller than in tennis and enclosed by glass walls, which can be used to hit balls off similar to squash.
Philippines player Malazarte said padel was “more like a chess match” than tennis.
“You have to open up the angle in order to win, you don’t rush the points,” she said.
“Whereas in tennis if you have a really good forehand, really good backhand, you can win a point.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Japan’s Teruaki Ando and Shinnosuke Nakamura (front) play a point against Lebanon’s Tamim El Hallak and Ralph Tohme during the men’s pairs padel first round match at the Nagoya City Highashi Sports Center in Nagoya on September 28, 2026. — AFP pic
Fully booked
Padel officials say the sport is enjoyed by people of all ages, and that 50 per cent of the worldwide playing population are women.
But not all sports that enjoy high playing numbers translate into successful spectator events.
Despite millions of players around the world squash failed with four bids to become an Olympic sport until it was finally added to the programme for the 2028 Los Angeles Games.
So is padel as much fun to watch as it is to play?
“When I watch tournaments live, from the first rounds, every year is getting more and more full,” said Kuwaiti player Mariam Al-Sarraj.
“Now it’s almost fully booked, so I feel like people like to watch it.”
The sport certainly won some new converts in Nagoya, with the crowd gasping in appreciation at some of the shots and rallies.
Interest was raised by the involvement of Japan’s Teruaki Ando and Shinnosuke Nakamura, who won a tense thriller against a pair from Lebanon.
IPF official Del Gaudio said padel’s Asian Games debut was “a source of pride” for everyone in the sport.
“It’s confirmation of padel’s growth worldwide,” she said.
“It represents a closer step to the Olympics.” — AFP
22501cdbd2c299e1: KOTA BHARU, Sept 28 — A common concern among traditional arts practitioners is the lack of successors to inherit their skills and knowledge as younger generations are often less inclined to carry on the art forms passed down by their parents.

However, Kelantan wayang kulit practitioner Kang Boon Ann, a Peranakan Chinese, has no such concerns — his entire family is actively involved in staging wayang kulit, a traditional form of shadow puppetry, performances.

Affectionately known as Che Ann, he is the founder of the Sri Cindayu Wayang Kulit Association and is among the state’s better-known non-Malay wayang kulit practitioners. Today, he and his family are working hard to preserve an art form more closely associated with the Malay community.

The family not only stages wayang kulit performances but also nurtures a new generation of practitioners. According to Che Ann, they are also making full use of modern communication technology to promote the centuries-old art form and keep it alive.
Primary school
Sharing his journey in wayang kulit, Che Ann, 58, said his interest in the traditional art was sparked while he was still in primary school.

Growing up in Kok Lanas at a time when television sets were not yet found in every household, he said wayang kulit was among the main forms of entertainment in the community, with performances often staged after the harvest season.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Kelantan ‘wayang kulit’ practitioner Kang Boon Ann, 58, who is also founder of the Sri Cindayu Wayang Kulit Association, displays a character he created after performing a ‘wayang kulit’ show at Tok Bali Jetty, Pasir Puteh. — Bernama pic

“I have been interested in wayang kulit since I was seven years old. There was no television back then. After the harvest season, villagers would stage wayang kulit performances and I would often accompany my grandmother to watch them.
“When I returned home, I would take my school exercise books and try to draw the puppets,” he told Bernama in an interview.
His fascination with the art was so strong that almost every page of his exercise books was eventually filled with sketches of wayang kulit puppets.

“My teacher used to scold me because the exercise book that was supposed to be used for homework was already filled with drawings. The only part without any drawing was the cover,” he recalled with a laugh.
From mechanic to ‘wayang kulit’ advocate
After completing his studies, Che Ann worked as a mechanic, but his passion for wayang kulit remained strong.
“I worked for 10 years before opening my own workshop in Kok Lanas. It was there that I met the late Tok Dalang Dollah Baju Merah. He taught me how to make the puppets,” he said.

Dollah Baju Merah, whose real name was Abdullah Ibrahim, was one of Kelantan’s renowned tok dalang, or wayang kulit puppeteers, and was highly regarded among practitioners for his skill in bringing a wide range of characters to life through his performances.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Kelantan ‘wayang kulit’ practitioner and Sri Cindayu Wayang Kulit Association founder Kang Boon Ann, 58, with his wife Eh Tian Eh Awang, 52, (second, right) and their children Kang Siew Lie, 32, (right) and Kang Xiau Ren, 29, (left), look at ‘wayang kulit’ characters used during a performance at Tok Bali Jetty, Pasir Puteh, recently. — Bernama pic
He died in September 2005 at the age of 67 due to health problems.

Che Ann said the late puppeteer taught him how to make puppets step by step for a year, from preparing and drying cowhide to crafting the puppets. Another puppeteer, the late Dollah Ramboo, taught him the art of performing wayang kulit for three years.
Che Ann later apprenticed under another craftsman Yusoff Mamat of Kampung Laut, Tumpat, to further hone his skills in producing coloured puppets.

According to Che Ann, he initially made wayang kulit puppets for his own personal collection. However, his skills attracted media attention, with reports about his work gradually bringing him wider recognition.

“Back then, I could see that wayang kulit was becoming increasingly subdued. There were fewer people performing it. That made me think that perhaps we should try to revive the art,” he said, adding that this was when he began dreaming of establishing his own wayang kulit troupe.
Family joins in
However, turning that dream into reality was not easy.

In 2005, Che Ann gathered several musicians to train them to play the various traditional Malay musical instruments used in folk ensembles such as wayang kulit. However, the effort did not last long as one by one, they stopped attending.
His wife Eh Tian Eh Awang, 52, then suggested an idea that would eventually change the course of their family’s journey.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Spectators watch a ‘wayang kulit’ performance by Sri Cindayu Wayang Kulit Association founder Kang Boon Ann, 58, at Tok Bali Jetty, Pasir Puteh, recently. — Bernama pic
“Fewer people from outside were coming for my training sessions. My wife said that instead of stopping our efforts, it would be better if our whole family learned to perform wayang kulit,” he said.

The suggestion marked a turning point. Che Ann began training his wife, two children and other family members to play the traditional musical instruments, manipulate the puppets and understand the various aspects of the wayang kulit performance.
Today, almost the entire performance is carried out by his family.
“Almost everyone in my family is involved. My wife used to play the gong, while the children played the musical instruments. Now, they can also perform as the tok dalang and teach others,” he said.
Legacy
Today, Che Ann’s children have mastered almost every aspect of the wayang kulit performance.
His daughter Kang Siew Lie, 32, or Lily, said she began attending training at the age of 14 and has never regretted continuing the family legacy.

“I feel that it would be such a waste if we did not continue this legacy because the knowledge is already right in front of us. Other people are willing to come and learn, so we ourselves need to become the successors to our father’s efforts,” she said.
In addition to playing the canang, Lily went on to master the gong, kesi and gedombak after furthering her studies in the performing arts.
For her, however, becoming a tok dalang presents a far greater challenge.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Sri Cindayu Wayang Kulit Association founder Kang Boon Ann’s son, Kang Xiau Ren, 29, performs a ‘wayang kulit’ show at Tok Bali Jetty, Pasir Puteh, recently. — Bernama pic

“Before becoming a tok dalang, you must first master the musical instruments. But the biggest challenge is producing different voices for the various (puppet) characters because female voices have certain limitations,” she said.
Her younger brother Kang Xiau Ren, 29, or Aaren, has emerged as a new-generation tok dalang who can switch between the role of puppeteer and musician depending on the requirements of a performance.
According to Aaren, training never ends because a tok dalang must constantly hone his skills.
“Even when I am driving, I would practise speaking in different voices,” he said, adding that a tok dalang needs more than just storytelling skills.

“One hand moves the puppet while the other searches for the next puppet. At the same time, your mind is thinking about the next scene, your mouth continues telling the story and your ears are listening to the rhythm of the music.
“Wayang kulit puppets are lifeless objects. We are the ones who bring them to life.”
Adapting heritage to the times
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Sri Cindayu Wayang Kulit Association founder Kang Boon Ann’s daughter, Kang Siew Lie, 32, skilfully plays a musical instrument during a wayang kulit performance, a traditional form of shadow puppetry, at Tok Bali Jetty, Pasir Puteh, recently. — Bernama pic
To keep wayang kulit relevant and appealing, the family has embraced social media while remaining committed to preserving the identity of the traditional art form.
Che Ann said TikTok has become an important platform for introducing wayang kulit to younger audiences.

“There have been people who watched us on TikTok and then came to meet us because they wanted to learn. This is what we want — for them to get to know wayang kulit first, and then develop an interest in it,” he said.
Aaren, meanwhile, has introduced several new elements, including digital sound effects, in the battle and archery scenes to enhance the audience’s experience.
“I do not want to change the tradition. I only add elements that can help the audience immerse themselves in the story, while the traditional music remains,” he said.
Beyond staging wayang kulit performances, the family also runs workshops at schools and educational institutions to nurture new practitioners.
Participants are introduced not only to the history of wayang kulit but also taught how to make puppets, play traditional musical instruments and stage performances.

While acknowledging that wayang kulit continues to face various challenges, including a shortage of successors and changing public tastes, Che Ann remains confident that the traditional art form still has a future.
He said for him, wayang kulit is no longer merely a personal passion but a responsibility to safeguard.

“I am not asking everyone to become a tok dalang. It is enough for them to know about wayang kulit. Once they know it, they will begin to appreciate it. And when they come to love it, they will make the effort to preserve it themselves,” he said. — Bernama

3549ba7f45f27e5e: Microsoft accidentally wiped some nonprofit customers' M365 data before their retention period expired – and now says it cannot tell them what disappeared, or even whether they lost anything. The cockup followed Microsoft's retirement of its Microsoft 365 Business Premium grant, which gave eligible nonprofits ten free licenses for the productivity suite. Microsoft announced in May 2025 that the grant would not renew after July 1 that year. It offered eligible nonprofits up to 300 free Microsoft 365 Business Basic licenses, alongside discounted pricing for plans including Business Premium. The company urged customers to move users onto another nonprofit plan before cancellation to avoid disruption or data loss. Organizations could also export anything they did not intend to retain in Microsoft 365. The problem arose after the subscriptions were deactivated. In an email to one affected customer seen by The Register, Microsoft admitted that, "due to an error," it had deleted remaining data before the retention and export window closed. Attempts to recover it had failed. "We have now investigated the recovery options, but unfortunately, the data cannot be recovered," Microsoft said. Redmond cannot determine what disappeared either. The company said it was "currently unable to provide a list showing which data may have been deleted or whether any data was deleted at all." It could say only that the problem involved expired Business Premium subscriptions. Microsoft confirmed the premature deletion to The Register. "After the applicable notice periods concluded and subscriptions were terminated, an error resulted in remaining data, if any, being deleted before the retention period had ended," a spokesperson said. "The impacted content would have been data associated with a customer's expired M365 Business Premium subscription." Microsoft did not say how many nonprofits were affected, how prematurely the deletion occurred, or what caused the error. The company said it regretted the impact and was offering affected nonprofits a free "concierge service," a meeting with a Microsoft specialist to help set up a new Microsoft 365 environment and answer questions. Useful if you need help building a shiny new environment. Less useful if what you really wanted was the data Microsoft deleted from the old one. ®

122ad487d91e2adb: A former US Army soldier has been sentenced to 70 months in prison for hacking telecoms companies, stealing sensitive records, and trying to extort more than $1 million from his victims. Cameron John Wagenius, 22, carried out the campaign while serving on active duty. He pleaded guilty in March 2025 to unlawfully transferring confidential phone records, then admitted conspiracy to commit wire fraud, computer-related extortion, and aggravated identity theft in a separate case that July. Court documents say Wagenius conspired with three others to obtain credentials for the protected networks of at least ten organizations between April 2023 and December 2024. During that period, he was stationed in South Korea and Texas. The Justice Department has not publicly identified the victims, describing them as US and overseas telecommunications companies and other organizations. Wagenius has also been linked to the 2024 Snowflake extortion campaign, which affected AT&T, Verizon, and numerous other companies, as The Register previously reported. After two suspects were arrested in connection with the Snowflake attacks, an account controlled by Wagenius claimed to possess AT&T call records belonging to Donald Trump and Kamala Harris. Using online aliases including "kiberphant0m," Wagenius and his co-conspirators obtained login credentials with a hacking tool he helped develop called SSH Brute, among other methods. They exchanged stolen credentials in Telegram group chats and discussed using them to gain unauthorized access to other parts of victims' networks. Court documents say the group traded hundreds of credentials and stole hundreds of thousands of customer records from multiple companies. Wagenius and his accomplices advertised stolen data through XSS, BreachForums, X, and Telegram. Some posts offered the information for sale, while others threatened to publish it unless victims paid. The Justice Department said the conspirators attempted to extort at least $1 million in total, successfully sold some stolen data, and used other records to commit fraud, including SIM swapping. US District Judge Lauren King told Wagenius at sentencing: "Your actions show a shocking disregard for the safety and security of the United States... You took these actions motivated by greed and a desire for notoriety." Wagenius was also ordered to pay $294,978 in restitution. ®

1d19e9f052572187: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 28 — After seven decades together, Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad today faced one of his most difficult moments as he accompanied his late wife, Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohd Ali, to her final resting place.
Dr Mahathir, who used a motorised wheelchair and wore an oxygen tube, remained present throughout the funeral rites as family members gathered to pay their last respects.

A sombre atmosphere marked the proceedings, from the family residence and the paying of last respects and funeral prayers at As-Syarif Mosque, Taman Sungai Besi Indah, to the Pusara Negara (National Cemetery), Precinct 20, Putrajaya.

Looking despondent, the former prime minister was seen gazing blankly for a moment at his wife’s remains while paying his last respects at the mosque before joining the funeral prayers, with thousands of congregants filling the mosque and spilling into the surrounding area.
Upon arriving at Pusara Negara, Tun Dr Mahathir watched as his wife’s remains were taken to the burial plot before she was laid to rest.

At official events and during more casual appearances, Dr Siti Hasmah was rarely far from her husband’s side, serving as his companion and a pillar of support throughout his life and political career.

f303c633186c16a6: BANGKOK, Sept 28 — Thailand’s Constitutional Court rejected today a challenge to the legality of ballots used in this year’s election, in a ruling that kept intact the decisive victory of Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.
The South-east Asian nation has a long history of political protests, military coups and court rulings that have unseated leaders.
The Constitutional Court has voided elections twice before. It could have nullified the February 8 election result and ordered a fresh vote, forcing Anutin’s coalition to face the electorate again.
But the court found QR codes and barcodes printed on the ballots did not violate the constitutional requirement of a secret vote, leaving Anutin’s conservative Bhumjaithai party at the helm.
“The court rules that the barcodes and QR codes are constitutional and do not violate the rights and freedoms of the voters,” judge Chiranit Havanond said.

Although the barcodes on party list ballots could theoretically be traced, the aim of the markings was to ensure electoral integrity, not to reveal which party individuals voted for, judge Sarawut Songsivilai said.
The case arose from more than 20 complaints made to the Office of the Ombudsman concerning the design of the paper ballots.
Petitioners had alleged that the QR codes and barcodes could have been used to identify individuals and how they voted, undermining ballot secrecy.
The court, however, said the Election Commission had maintained voter secrecy by keeping ballot stubs that identified voters separate from the portion of the ballots that were cast.
Anutin’s Bhumjaithai won handily in February, consolidating rural political clans and riding a wave of nationalism following deadly border clashes with Cambodia last year.
But while it took the most constituencies, Bhumjaithai failed to win an outright majority and joined forces with third-place Pheu Thai, the populist party of former prime minister Thaksin Shinawatra.

In 2006, the Constitutional Court invalidated snap polls — which were boycotted by the opposition — ruling the election date was unfairly chosen and voting booths had compromised the secrecy of the ballot.
The court also annulled the 2014 election on the grounds that voting was not held for the entire country on the same day — after anti-government protesters disrupted polling sites.

Both years saw huge protests followed by military coups that ousted a Shinawatra — Thaksin first, and his sister Yingluck in 2014, part of a long struggle between the populist political dynasty and conservative elites. — afp

902ba67841dcb297: Ofcom has blocked an Openreach discount for bringing customers onto its fiber network, warning that rivals might be unable to match the price and recover their costs. The "Incremental New to Openreach Customer Offer" was one of several pricing changes due to take effect on October 1. It is the first Openreach commercial offer the regulator has rejected; the others can proceed. Openreach, BT's functionally separate network division and Britain's largest fixed-line infrastructure provider, notified Ofcom of the pricing plans in June. The rejected offer would have rewarded internet service providers (ISPs) for connecting more new fiber-to-the-premises (FTTP) customers to Openreach than an agreed baseline. Ofcom provisionally decided to block the offer in July and consulted the industry. It has now made that decision permanent. The watchdog concluded that the charges were "not fair and reasonable" because a reasonably efficient rival might be unable to match them while recovering its costs. It was particularly concerned about alternative network operators, or altnets, which need to attract customers to grow and compete with Openreach. Openreach proposed a £35 connection discount and a monthly reduction of up to £9.50 for as long as 30 months, applying only to customers above each ISP's normal level of new Openreach signups. Ofcom said the scale and targeting of the discount could impede altnets' efforts to build their customer bases. Ofcom allowed Openreach's other proposed discounts to proceed. These include a one-off £50 rebate for connections above an ISP's usual number of new Openreach customers in areas served by Virgin Media O2. Altnets also operate in some of those areas, but Ofcom judged the smaller discount unlikely to harm long-term competition. It said the offer's geographical targeting therefore did not amount to undue discrimination. Another offer gives communications providers a free connection when net new Ethernet demand exceeds 90 percent of their historical run rate. Ofcom concluded its conditions would not impede the use of rival networks and the pricing raised no "prima facie concerns" requiring further investigation. Ofcom previously declined to intervene in Openreach discount schemes including Equinox and Equinox 2, which were intended to encourage ISPs to migrate customers from copper to FTTP. Reaction to Ofcom's decision was mixed. Wholesale fiber operator nexfibre called it a positive step toward protecting competition in the UK market, but said the regulator could have gone further. "Openreach's tactic of drip-feeding price changes via special offers needs to stop at a time when competition remains nascent. Ensuring alternative networks have the incentives to invest, grow and achieve scale will be critical to creating credible, sustainable competition," nexfibre said in a statement. Virgin Media O2 also welcomed the intervention, despite Ofcom allowing the geographically targeted offer aimed at areas where it operates. "Although we believe the regulator could have gone further, we welcome Ofcom's move to clip Openreach's wings on its most aggressive offer and looking ahead it is crucial the dominant incumbent's behaviour is fully kept in check as meaningful wholesale competition emerges," a spokesperson told us. Openreach appeared sanguine about the ruling. "Ofcom's decision not to approve our incremental FTTP new to Openreach offer is in line with their consultation position. We put this offer forward in good faith to help our customers compete and deliver better value for households," said James Lowther, Openreach managing director for commercial. "While we continue to believe the offer would have benefited customers and competition, we'll review the decision carefully and continue to engage constructively with Ofcom and our customers." ®

ec31b05540f90960: IPOH, Sept 28 — Perak is hoping for at least RM1.4 billion in the upcoming Federal Budget to fund key water supply infrastructure, particularly a project to transfer water from Sungai Perak to Bukit Merah to support farmers regularly affected by drought.
Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Saarani Mohamad said the project was among the state’s priorities submitted by the Perak Economic Planning Unit to the Finance Ministry ahead of the Budget announcement.

“We are currently in the phase of realising the project to transfer water from Sungai Perak to Bukit Merah. If there is surplus water later, only then will we consider selling treated water to Penang.
“This is expected to help meet water needs in Kerian Integrated Green Industrial Park in northern Perak, including for farmers who, as we know, face problems every time there is a drought,” he said.

Saarani said this in a press conference when asked about state government’s wish list ahead of Federal Budget, at the launching of the 2MW Biogas Renewable Energy Plant at the Lahat Sanitary Landfill here.
Saarani said the project was expected to be operational by around 2030 or 2031 if it proceeded according to schedule.
“Hopefully, it will be included in this year’s Budget,” he said.
He said the project would involve two main components, with the first involving infrastructure such as pumps and water tunnels.

“This infrastructure should be funded by the Federal Government through the Energy Transition and Water Transformation Ministry, with the necessary infrastructure works falling under the federal government’s responsibility through National Water Services Commission,” he said.
Saarani said the second component could be financed through Khazanah Air Perak, a consortium involving the state government and a subsidiary of the Perak State Agricultural Development Corporation.
“We can use loans, either from the federal government, through private finance initiative financing or from banks.
“But this can only be done once the infrastructure is in place,” he said.
Saarani said the infrastructure was crucial as the state had already identified the route for transporting water from Sungai Perak.
“We need pumps to draw the water and tunnels to transport it. This is expensive and needs to be started. That is the most important thing for us,” he said.
He said the estimated cost for the infrastructure alone was between RM1.4 billion and RM2 billion, excluding other components of the project.
“The longer we delay, the more expensive the materials will become,” he said.
Meanwhile, Saarani said the state government had also identified several urgent needs involving schools during a recent state development meeting.
He said one of the immediate concerns was the need for additional buildings at existing schools where six- and seven-year-old pupils would be entering Year One simultaneously next year.
“Therefore, there is a need to construct additional buildings,” he said.
Saarani said another concern involved dilapidated school buildings, with the state government receiving complaints from school principals and parent-teacher associations.
“There are many buildings that are already in poor condition, and this is beyond the capacity of the state government,” he said.
He said Perak also needed new schools in areas experiencing rapid development, particularly new growth areas.
“Whenever new development projects take place, there will be a need for new housing areas. Every new housing development should provide a location for a school.
“Schools are very important. We do not want schools operating in two sessions. We want single-session schools and schools that provide a comfortable environment for students to learn,” he said.

5c192c8c341873e2: PUTRAJAYA, Sept 28 — The remains of the late Tun Dr Hasmah Mohd Ali have been laid to rest at the National Mausoleum in Precinct 20, Putrajaya.
The burial was witnessed by droves of supporters, as well as family members and friends who gathered to pay their final respects.

Mourners gathered around the grave as Dr Hasmah’s remains were lowered into the grave, followed by the recitation of the talqin, a traditional Islamic rite that reminds the deceased of the tenets of faith, and prayers led by Masjid Putra Grand Imam Muhamad Zakuwa Rodzali.

The state funeral procession continued with the sprinkling of fragrant flower petals and leaves, known as bunga rampai, and rose water by former prime minister Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad, Dr Hasmah’s husband, followed by their children and other family members.
Later, the immediate family was presented with the Jalur Gemilang by Official Government Ceremonies Committee chairman Datuk Abd Shukor Mahmood.

c005ce19c05e5f54: GUNUNG JERAI, Sept 28 — German rider Lennart Jasch etched his name into the record books of Le Tour de Langkawi (LTdL) by winning the first-ever summit finish at Gunung Jerai, claiming Stage 2 and taking the overall leader’s jersey.

The 25-year-old Tudor Pro Cycling Team clocked 3:37:21 over the 145.6-kilometre (km) route from Taiping, taking over from Stage 1 winner Matteo Malucelli of XDS Astana Team at the top of the General Classification.

“Of course super happy. Just one week since I won the last race. Just feels incredible and I need to thank the team so much. They did such an amazing job. I was never further back than maybe position three on the climb. It was just such a strong team effort. So yeah, really thank you, team,” he said after the stage, today.

Jasch launched his attack with about two kilometres remaining to close down to Abel Balderstone of Caja Rural-Seguros RGA, before overtaking the Spaniard in the closing stages to win ahead of Balderstone, who finished second in 3:37:37, while teammate Jan Castellon was third in 3:37:53.
Knowing that Balderstone was also at his limit as he closed the gap, Jasch went “full gas” and used his superior pace to overtake his rival in the final stretch.

The former speed skater’s ascent also earned him the King of the Mountains (KOM) polka dot jersey with 15 points, while his cumulative time of 7:44:04 put him at the top of the General Classification.

“Of course super special, also super special to have three wins in one season as a neo-pro. I don’t know, maybe you have the statistics how many people won three pro races in one year, but I think there are not so many, so I’m super super happy that I could pull this off and I got all the support from the team,” he said.

Asked about his chances of winning the overall title, Jasch remained cautious, saying that there are still six stages left, including two difficult mountain stages and that he preferred to take the race day by day until conclusion.

Meanwhile, Italian sprinter Malucelli retained the blue jersey for the sprinters classification with 17 points, ahead of Modern Adventure Pro Cycling’s Riley Pickrell on 12 points and Fernando Gaviria of Caja Rural-Seguros RGA on nine.

In the Best Asian Rider contest, Aisan Racing Team’s Yuhi Todome, a bronze medallist at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games took the white jersey with an overall time of 7:49:04s while Kee Zhe Yie of Terengganu Cycling Team finished as Malaysia’s best finisher of the day.
Tomorrow’s Stage 3 will see the peloton tackle a 189.7km route from Sungai Petani to Kuala Kangsar featuring three sprints in Kuala Ketil, Lawin dan Sauk. — Bernama
405ef38359170223: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 28 — Malaysia’s domestic financial markets continued to adjust in an orderly manner, supported by balanced two-way flows that ensured effective price intermediation among market participants, according to Bank Negara Malaysia’s Financial Markets Committee (FMC).
The “Discussion Summary” of the FMC Meeting 2/2026 revealed that market conditions remained conducive for corporates to raise funds to meet their financing requirements.

“Looking ahead, external factors such as geopolitical uncertainties, oil price volatility and an evolving global interest rate environment remain near-term headwinds for the domestic market. However, members noted that the recent increase in bond yields may present an attractive entry point for foreign investors, given that investor sentiment towards Malaysia continues to be favourable,” the FMC said.

It added that these factors, alongside ongoing measures such as the qualified resident investor programme and engagement with government-linked companies, government-linked investment companies and corporates to repatriate and convert their foreign currency income, are expected to provide continued support for the foreign exchange and bond markets.
The FMC also said recent movements in the domestic financial markets were driven primarily by global factors, particularly developments in the US policy rate.

“Growing prospects of higher US interest rates and the actual realisation of a rate hike by the US Federal Reserve led to a stronger US dollar and higher US Treasury yields. These, in turn, resulted in broad-based adjustments across global markets, including regional currencies and bonds,” it added.

On the currency, it noted that the ringgit moderated in September after remaining largely stable in July and August, while Malaysian Government Securities yields also increased following a prolonged period of relative stability. This came amid a broader repricing of global interest rate expectations and higher global bond yields.
Members of the committee also observed robust interest in corporate bond issuance and increased hedging activity. — Bernama
e001216143681d5a: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 28 — Bursa Malaysia ended marginally lower today amid selling activity as the market lacked fresh catalysts to spur investors’ buying interest, an analyst said.
At 5 pm, the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) eased 1.60 points, or 0.09 per cent, to 1,670.02, from Friday’s close of 1,671.62.
The benchmark index, which opened 0.93 of-a-point higher at 1,672.55, moved between 1,668.61 and 1,674.11 throughout the trading session.
Market breadth was negative as losers surpassed gainers 748 to 388, while 517 counters were unchanged, 1,271 untraded and 91 suspended.
Turnover slipped to 3.11 billion units worth RM2.40 billion from 4.07 billion units valued at RM2.69 billion on Friday.

Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said the stockbroking firm maintained a cautious view of the market as persistent external headwinds and foreign selling could limit near-term upside.

“Nevertheless, the recent market correction has brought valuations of selected blue-chip stocks to more attractive levels, which could encourage bargain hunting, particularly among fundamentally strong heavyweights.
“Hence, we expect trading to remain selective, with buying interest likely to emerge on further weakness,” he told Bernama.
As such, he anticipated the FBM KLCI to trend within the 1,660-1,690 range for the week.

Berjaya Research Sdn Bhd head of research Kenneth Leong said market attention will also turn to US job openings and consumer confidence data due tomorrow, which could influence expectations for the Federal Reserve’s policy path and global risk appetite.
“A softer-than-expected set of readings may offer some relief to equities, but signs of resilient labour demand or weakening consumer sentiment could add to market volatility,” he said.
