5eaf464e45df768f: The world’s most important shipping lanes pass through the Strait of Malacca.
Yet, within Malaysia’s maritime boundaries, there is no single framework to determine who gets to use which patch of water and for what purpose.

That shortcoming was the subject of discussion at a recent Ensearch forum “Our Seas, Our Future” where Dr Gopinath Nagaraj and Dr Harinder Rai Singh of FanLi Marine and Consultancy Sdn Bhd (FanLi) made the case for marine spatial planning with a clarity Malaysia would do well to heed.
Their framing of the sea as overlapping estates of biodiversity, fisheries, industry and maritime activity is right. The ocean is not just a shipping lane with some fish in it.
Their point is that fragmented governance, rather than a lack of awareness, is the real barrier.

The numbers bear this out: fisheries production was valued at RM11.43 billion in 2023, Malaysian ports handled more than 30 million TEUs in 2024, and offshore oil, gas and tourism all draw on the same finite waters.
Yet each sector is planned or managed by a different authority under a different law.
Fragmentation is not a natural disaster. It is a choice — the accumulated result of agencies guarding their own turf and a Cabinet unwilling to make one give ground.
The department of environment approves reclamation and coastal EIA reports one environmental impact assessment at a time. That is not enough.

Every silted estuary and buried mudflat in this country may have been approved through a valid EIA. Until the DOE requires cumulative-impact assessments — measuring the combined effect of projects along an entire coastline rather than assessing each project in isolation — its approval process risks certifying decline one project at a time.

The fisheries numbers tell another story. In 2022, marine landings totalled 1.308 million metric tonnes (mt), valued at RM11.3 billion. In 2023, they fell to 1.27 million mt, valued at RM11.43 billion. In 2024, they rose to 1.392 million mt, valued at RM11.84 billion, and in 2025 to 1.393 million mt, valued at RM11.88 billion.

The fisheries department holds the nursery-ground data any marine plan would need. Yet there is still no publicly available national fish-habitat atlas. Food security is its responsibility. Where is the map?
The marine department and the transport ministry plan sea lanes and port expansions as though reefs and fishing grounds simply are not there.
Navigation matters enormously, but it is not the only estate at sea. Too often, the ministry behaves like the senior claimant whose needs are settled before anyone else is consulted.
The malaysian maritime enforcement agency and the navy have the mandate to secure our waters. Yet illegal sand dredging, unpermitted reclamation and foreign incursions continue.
This is the half of the conversation too often forgotten: a marine plan without enforcement is a coloured map. Zoning that no one polices protects nothing.
State governments control the foreshore out to three nautical miles and monetise it through reclamation deals that federal ecological policy struggle to stop.

Every attempt at a “national” ocean policy eventually runs into this constitutional divide. Sabah, Sarawak and reclamation-hungry peninsular states cannot keep hiding behind the Federal Constitution while treating the coastline as an asset to be sold to the highest bidder.
PlanMalaysia (formerly known as the department of town and country planning) and local authorities have been told to extend spatial planning into marine areas.
Yet they lack both the statutory machinery and the planning expertise to do so effectively. Beyond the high-water line, they have done little.
Petronas operates across the same seabed designated for conservation, under terms negotiated federally, without having to reconcile its footprint within an integrated marine plan.
Its data can also become difficult to scrutinise when national security is invoked.
And above all sits the Cabinet. The draft National Ocean Policy, with its proposal for an oceans and fisheries ministry, has remained a draft for years.

This is not a technical shortfall. It is a decision no one has been willing to make because unification means one ministry losing authority to another. That is a failure of political will dressed up as a coordination problem.
The experts who advocated for marine spatial planning (MSP) can only diagnose and recommend.

Their prescription is sound: a national MSP governance unit with a real legal mandate; a marine data system and conflict atlas; pilot planning zones in Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah and Sarawak; and zoning developed through genuine consultation with fisherfolk who actually know the waters. It is the right blueprint.

But blueprints have never been the problem. Malaysia does not lack marine policy; it has too much of it, scattered across a dozen agencies, with none willing to surrender an inch and no single body empowered to force them to work together.
So the test is simple, and it is a test of government, not consultants.
Give one body three things: a legal mandate strong enough to override sectoral silos, a budget line in the next Malaysia Plan, and enforcement teeth on the water.
Most importantly, give it a political structure capable of bringing competing interests together.
The draft National Ocean Policy advocated such an approach. Drawing on a similar challenge faced by Canada, it proposed a ministry of oceans and fisheries.
Anything less, and the next forum will be another well-attended description of a problem we have all agreed on for a decade — held while the reclamation barges keep working just offshore.
The sea is a shared and finite national asset, not empty space reserved for the most powerful claimant. Right now, it has no ministry, no map and no enforcer of its own.
That is not the ocean’s failing. It is ours.

ce70dbb38957bdd7: I saw a social media post about a man so old he’s bent double but still doing motorcycle food delivery. Most comments on the post were positive and laudatory, seeing this as evidence that, in spite of advanced age, some people still want to be useful and be seen as “normal”.
Yeah, as normal as old people in developed countries working as cashiers at convenience stores or cleaning tables at fast-food joints.
I don’t buy that. If somebody of that age and physical condition is still running around delivering food, they aren’t doing it for fun or for the flex.

I'm a retiree. I’m not rich but I think I have “enough”, whatever enough is. It could turn out I don’t actually have enough and will end my days burdening others or, just as bad in my view, that I have more than enough -- which means I’ve wasted too much of my life acquiring wealth and not actually living it.

May I be spared these two calamities. I’m more inclined to believe that not having enough is the real reason the old bent-double man still runs around doing food deliveries. He’s not doing it for the fresh air or to meet new people.

And may you be spared that fate, too. Life gets tougher every day and not a single day passes that I don’t think about my good fortune of having retired and being able to approach 70 in relatively good physical and economic health. I also can’t help but think of those worse off than me every single day.

In the old days people didn’t really retire. They just stopped working when their body couldn’t handle it any more or when their grown-up children started taking care of them. Those who had actual pensions, mostly retired government employees, were the extra lucky ones.

I chose to retire in my early 60s with a year of my employment contract still to run. Things were changing at my employer's - the usual corporate transformation stuff - and it was best I left and let the new bosses choose my replacement themselves.

In effect I had a year-long pre-retirement leave: I have nothing to complain about and plenty to be grateful for. But some of my corporate peers chose to continue working, and I doubt it’s because they need the money. I surmise they need the job as a validation of some sorts – that 'Hey, I'm still needed and relevant and important'!

I don’t miss the good old corporate warrior days. What I do miss is the interaction with people at work, which I replace by making new friends while still keeping the old ones. Many still remember me and I never say no to a chance for a free meal and listen to them whinge about their bosses!

Through my career, I never took myself seriously. I earned enough to live a comfortable life and feed and clothe and educate my kids. My four decades of being a pen-pusher also gave me “enough” for my retirement, which I think is what running the rat race should be about.

Malaysia is still a country of young people but as lifespans increase there are an increasing number of people like me, comfortably retired and with years still ahead of us. But there are also many others like that old man who, allegedly, still does motorcycle delivery in spite of his advanced age and medical condition.

Having “enough” helps you be independent. There is life outside of work and that spared me the pain of leaving my title, office, and other perks behind. After all I wasn’t teaching the young or curing the sick or growing food or keeping society safe through unglamorous jobs as firemen or rubbish collectors. What I did for a living wasn’t really fundamental to the survival of our species.

Many middle-aged people, especially government servants, pray for an optional early retirement that can't come early enough. They’re probably stuck in a toxic work environment just to put food on the table and perhaps squirrel away some money for retirement. That’s not living - that’s just surviving.

That we’re a country of many young people still toiling away to create wealth for themselves, and hence for the country, is a blessing. Their labour ensures that our pension funds and investments and social safety nets such as public healthcare will still last at least for a few more decades.

However, the younger generation are not guaranteed a safety net and soft landing when they retire. We post-WW2 “Baby Boomers” are the wealthiest generation ever, but we may need that wealth to take care of ourselves and not burden our own children, whose own wealth and filial piety may not be enough to care for us.

Our generation’s wealth also unfortunately comes from destructive greed. We live a better life than our parents but the price of our good life comes from ruining the climate and depleting and defiling the earth’s resources and creating economic and social disparities. Such is the world we’re handing to our kids.

Apart from relationships and independence, health matters more as we age. We once traded our time and even health to make money. Now, we’re trying to trade money for time and health. But time and health are elusive and without some humility in our life perspectives, they still can’t guarantee a peaceful autumn of our life.

Ironically a solution for a happier final chapter perhaps lies in giving back to others. When I recall the old Japanese rescue workers at the Fukushima nuclear plant disaster as well as the elderly British protesters against the Gaza genocide who volunteered to be arrested in the UK, I choke up.

These brave old people purposely chose harm and danger for themselves to protect those younger than themselves. They had a good innings in the game of life, and are now willing to sacrifice to help the younger ones play their own innings. It’s the ultimate measure of having lived a good life that you’re prepared to lose it to protect others.

I’m extremely lucky I never had to make such a decision, or even have to be on a motorcycle to deliver food. I’d like to think I’d have discharged myself honourably if tested. But I’m in no hurry to put myself to these tests!

e6adf117654cb8c3: Benighted politics are once again haunting the Balkans. This month’s semi-official funeral in Belgrade for the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić, whom many Bosnian Serbs still honour, has dredged up past traumas and reignited nationalist tensions. Diplomatic relations between Serbia and Bosnia are deteriorating, casting further doubt on Serbia’s already semi-stalled accession to the European Union.

Worse, while Europe and the US used to be mostly aligned in their support for the tenuous political process in Bosnia, that is no longer the case. Whereas previous US presidents might have been accused of being overly interventionist, Donald Trump’s administration has shown no interest in the region’s delicate political processes whatsoever. Its sole concern is to advance narrow economic interests, and this has meant tolerating or even supporting hardline Serbian nationalists in Bosnia.

For example, the Trump administration has thrown its support behind a gas pipeline that would connect the Croatian coast to Sarajevo (the Bosnian capital). At first glance, such a project makes sense, given its potential to alleviate the region’s dependence on Russian gas. But when contracts may suspiciously be awarded to a previously unknown company whose leaders have “personal connections to Donald Trump,” warning lights start flashing.

Warning lights are flashing on the political front, too. Bosnia will hold elections this October, and depending on the outcome, hardline Serb forces may join with hardline Croats to change the country’s governance framework. The timing for such a gambit is ideal because the US obviously would look the other way. But should it succeed, the Bosniak (Muslim) community is bound to feel threatened and will respond accordingly. That would increase the risk of a downward spiral that could profoundly destabilise the country.

Moreover, Serbia will also hold elections in October. After years of mass student protests, the government is facing a broad grassroots opposition movement, which is now organised under the banner of the “Student List”. With the outcome still far from certain, one can easily imagine a scenario in which President Aleksandar Vučić’s populist regime simply declares victory, triggering even more instability.

The situation in Kosovo is no calmer. Reconciliation talks between Serbia and Kosovo have stalled, and local authorities in the divided town of Mitrovica have yet to be given responsibility for the bridge linking the Serbian and Albanian districts, owing to fears of what might follow.

More broadly, the country’s political system is deadlocked, and anger over the Kosovo Specialist Chambers’ recent conviction of Hashim Thaci, a former military leader who served as president of Kosovo from 2016 to 2020, has further alienated the country from its previous international partners.

None of these developments would necessarily be destabilising on its own. But taken together, they risk creating a critical mass of nationalist sentiment. The central idea behind the peace processes a quarter-century ago was that a combination of EU accession talks and reconciliation facilitated by various international tribunals would gradually bring stability and cooperation to the region. But that hope has not been vindicated.

With the exception of Montenegro, and possibly Albania, integration into the EU has stalled and lost much of its power as a motivating force. Equally disappointing, the proceedings led by international tribunals at The Hague have been so grotesquely drawn out as to have no chance of promoting reconciliation. They may even be making the situation worse.

Tiny Montenegro is still on a promising trajectory, but whether its EU accession bid could survive a new whirlwind of regional turmoil is far from certain. If Serbia has an interest in destabilising its neighbour, it can easily do so.

As is always the case in the Balkans, there are no easy solutions to address the rising tensions. Each country has its own political processes, but the risk of mutually reinforcing spillovers is high. With the US focussed solely on private economic interests, and with the EU distracted by Russian aggression and US unpredictability, the prospects for coherent international policies to restore stability, promote reconciliation, and support integration are bleak.

This doesn’t mean we are heading towards a new round of Balkan wars. But even limited skirmishes could be sufficient to push the entire region onto a more uncertain and dangerous path. Political leaders, particularly in Europe, must heed the alarm. The Balkans brought major wars to Europe twice in the previous century, and they could easily create instability in this century, too.
Carl Bildt is a former prime minister and foreign minister of Sweden.

4e709fa953bde058: In November 2021, the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History opened an exhibit called “The Electric Dr. Franklin,” describing “Benjamin Franklin’s pioneering contributions to electrical science.” The exhibit explained that, prior to becoming an abolitionist, he had enslaved people in his household. “Benjamin Franklin’s remarkable scientific accomplishments were, in part, enabled by slavery,” it declared.

The exhibit speculated that Franklin may have used enslaved people in his electrical research. “Franklin wrote about experiments in which he took shocks and used family and friends in these ways, although he seldom identified who in particular assisted him,” stated the exhibit, which closed in 2025 but can still be found online. “Indentured servants and enslaved people in his household could also have been used, although we may never know for certain.”

914bb2017c706e9d: Thirty years after Apple abandoned Copland, its doomed attempt to create a modern Mac operating system, a new emulator lets you try the final developer build in your browser. Copland was intended to replace Apple's System 7 with a PowerPC-native operating system built around a microkernel, protected memory, and preemptive multitasking for system services. Three unfinished developer builds – D7E1, D9, and D11E4 – are publicly known. Relatively few people outside Apple's developer community in the mid-1990s ever had the opportunity to use them. Now you can boot Apple Copland D11E4 in your browser and explore the unstable prerelease OS without installing anything. Developer Michael Steil, also known as Mist, made it possible with an experimental fork of the DingusPPC Power Mac emulator. Steil says the 11 patches that enable DingusPPC to boot Copland were written with AI assistance. The upstream project does not accept AI-assisted patches, so the fixes would have to be rewritten before they could be incorporated. Don't expect miracles. The emulator runs D11E4, the final build Apple distributed to developers, dating from June 1996. It remains very much unfinished: if the emulated system hits an assertion, it drops into a debugger and asks the user to continue manually. Apple CEO Gil Amelio had demonstrated Copland at the company's 1995 Worldwide Developers Conference, but the project never approached the stability required for release. Much of Copland existed as plans and documentation rather than finished code. In 2009, Steil assembled an extensive archive of that material in Apple Copland Reference Documentation. There was also a planned successor to Copland, codenamed Gershwin, but it remained nothing more than a plan. The modern Gershwin desktop we covered a year ago is a nod to that nonexistent OS. Anyone familiar with the classic Mac OS of the late 1990s will recognize parts of Copland, and for good reason. Copland overran so badly that Amelio recruited the late Ellen Hancock from IBM as Apple's chief technology officer and tasked her with getting the project back on track. After reviewing its progress, she instead recommended cancelling it and acquiring an operating system elsewhere. Apple considered several alternatives, including acquiring Be for BeOS and working with Sun on a system based on Solaris. It ultimately bought NeXT, bringing Steve Jobs back to the company along with NeXTSTEP. Hancock was later sidelined under Jobs and resigned in 1997. Apple acquired NeXT at the end of 1996, just months after cancelling Copland. The first developer release of its NeXTSTEP-based successor, Rhapsody, followed in 1997 – continuing the musical codenames, if not the code. Rhapsody evolved into Mac OS X Server 1.0 in 1999 and the consumer release of Mac OS X 10.0 in 2001. Replacing the Mac OS architecture took years. While that work continued, Apple folded some of Copland's more mature components into updates to its existing operating system. Mac OS 8, released in 1997, gained Copland's Platinum interface and a PowerPC-native, multithreaded Finder. Its Appearance control panel supported themes, although Apple shipped only Platinum. Renaming what had been planned as Mac OS 7.7 also helped Apple end the clone program, whose licensing agreements covered System 7. Mac OS 8.1 followed in 1998 with HFS+, Apple's new format for larger disks. Later that year, Mac OS 8.5 became the first PowerPC-only release. Further pieces of Copland's work appeared across Mac OS 8 and 9, allowing Apple to improve the old platform while Mac OS X was being prepared. When Apple bought NeXT, NeXTSTEP already ran on Motorola 680x0, Intel x86, Sun SPARC and HP PA-RISC processors. That portable foundation later helped Apple move the Mac to Intel, while OS X became the basis for the operating systems used by the iPhone and iPad. Apple's future might have looked very different had Copland succeeded. Now it's easier than ever to see why it didn't. ®
d2dfe33bda6046d1: Big AI has a problem. Its companies must ingest other people’s work. You know, books, news stories, photographs, code, websites, that one original meme you came up with, and practically everything else on the internet to train its large language models (LLMs). We all know that. We also know that AI companies hate paying for any of it, obeying the licenses attached to it, or, God forbid, sharing their revenue with the companies and people who created the work in the first place. Recently, Big AI's default way of doing business: "Take it now, argue about legality later," has become more in your face than ever. Look, for example, at the copyright fight between The New York Times and OpenAI and Microsoft. According to 404 Media’s reporting on recently unsealed court documents - arguments from the plaintiffs that the court has not yet ruled on - Microsoft allegedly knew what it was doing when it was importing the internet willy-nilly. Microsoft's Director of Applied Science, Dr. Brent Hecht, was quoted in the news plaintiffs' 92-page combined brief as saying: the case was about “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions." Indeed, it was possibly the “largest theft of labor in human history,” he was quoted as saying in the summary judgment brief from the journalists' lawyers [PDF].This, mind you, wasn't a comment by a member of the press; it was from a senior Microsoft staffer. Hecht wasn't the only one at Microsoft who commented. In an internal Microsoft policy document also quoted in the court papers, the authors admitted generative AI could “significantly disrupt the employment of the very people who generated the data on which the foundation model was trained [because] LLMs are a product that destroys its supply chain.” That, in turn, leads to model collapse. Ironically, AI is killing the content-creator goose that lays the gold eggs of worthwhile content. Judge Sidney H. Stein of the US District Court for the Southern District of New York has not yet issued a decision on the case. OpenAI and Microsoft are actively disputing the plaintiffs' allegations under a "fair use" defense. They contend that using public articles and books to train large language models helps push forward public knowledge, and isn't acting as a "unlawful economic market substitute". But the statements the documents cites are real. Big AI knows it needs the content. Some of the companies concerned don't give a damn; money now, worry later is their motto. Those who can look past the revenue numbers are well aware they're engaged in what Microsoft itself called a “doom loop” of AI content strategy in those unsealed court documents. Will that stop them? Nah. According to the filing [PDF], which refers to sworn deposition testimony of OpenAI’s own corporate representative, it also testified that its LLMs were happy to vacuum up other people's work even when a paywall nominally protected it. Its rep was quoted as saying they were unaware of “any effort to detect paywall content in its training datasets” or “to remove paywall content from its training datasets.” When OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman was told OpenAI could hack its way through the firewall, he responded, “ah, nice.” Whether or not these statements are found to be reflective of a wider attitude, similar attitudes prevail amongst Big AI. Such policies could eventually come back and bite the LLM makers; it's already affecting the market for journalism, fiction writing, graphics creation, anything that demands humans actually get paid for producing original work. But Big AI just doesn't want to pay for it. That's not a side effect. It's the business model. Joe User couldn't care less. They just want a quick answer that sounds right. Some of them couldn't care less about getting the right answers. As for looking deeper to see if the information they're regurgitating is accurate, forget about it! As an OpenAI software engineer put it: “No matter how prominently we show the links, users won’t click.” Well, I click. That's a big reason why Perplexity is my AI of choice. It's not that it gives a more reliable answer. No, it's that, unlike most LLMs, Perplexity provides sources and links, and I check them before accepting what it tells me. But then I'm a journalist whose degrees are in history, where my professors drummed into me that you always - always - look at the primary sources. Big AI takes the same approach with its code generators. The US Ninth Circuit recently handed GitHub, Microsoft, and OpenAI a narrow win in the Doe v. GitHub lawsuit. The court ruled that the plaintiffs hadn't established a claim under one particular provision of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), which concerns the removal or alteration of copyright-management information (CMI). In short, the court said that generating new code without including CMI is not necessarily the same thing as removing or altering copyright information from an existing work. Judge Eric Miller wrote: “One who creates a new work and fails to include CMI cannot be said to have ‘removed’ or ‘altered’ anything.” This ruling didn't establish that GitHub Copilot or any other coding model may train on every open source project without restriction. It didn't determine that copying source code into a training set is always fair use. It did not decide that generated code cannot infringe copyright. And it certainly did not repeal the GPL, Apache, BSD, MIT, or any other open-source license. After all, open source isn't a synonym for “do whatever you want with it.” It just seems that way when AI gets its hands on open source code. That's the problem with AI-generated code. A programmer who receives a Copilot suggestion is very unlikely to check whether the GPL covers the code, or whether Apache covers the snippet from a library. The developer certainly can't tell which license terms may apply to the code that just popped up from Opus 5.5 or GPT 6. As the guy from OpenAI said, people don't click the links, and in AI-enabled programming pipelines, they don't even have the links anyway. An open source-savvy attorney friend of mine has a bigger worry than this narrow decision. He told me that what gives him "pause is a broader trend. There are multiple cases where parties are litigating open source licenses as contracts rather than as the IP / copyright licenses they were written to be. Contract theories let a plaintiff sidestep the questions copyright forces you to answer. 'Do you own the work? Is it protectable expression? Was it actually copied?'" He added: "Those questions are the foundation on which licenses are built. Open source licenses are grants of permission to use someone's intellectual property. If a case can't show that any intellectual property was owned or infringed, it's fair to ask whether enforcing the license as a bare contract supports open source licensing or quietly turns it into something else." With AI in the mix, this issue will eventually become one of those nasty IP matters developers hate, businesses want to avoid, but that courts must settle with expensive lawyers whose hourly rates worry even AI millionaires. After all, IP uncertainty isn't a minor paperwork issue. It is a supply-chain security and compliance problem. If you use AI-generated code, you may be importing unknown legal obligations into your software. If you are an open-source developer, your work may be used to improve a proprietary service that returns code without provenance, attribution, or meaningful reciprocity. And if you are a customer, you may be relying on software whose origins no one can fully explain. The Ninth Circuit ruling didn't solve any of that. We're in for a lot more open source litigation that will make SCO vs. the known Linux universe look like a kerfuffle over a parking ticket. Then there is the latest wrinkle: A federal antitrust lawsuit against Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI, and Google. The plaintiffs allege the companies coordinated to slow the development of advanced AI systems. The lawsuit points to public statements from AI leaders all calling for coordination to “pace” frontier AI development over a single weekend. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has argued for industry-wide coordination to slow frontier development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis, and Elon Musk have also publicly expressed versions of the view that powerful AI systems need controls and careful deployment. On its face, that sounds sensible. AI safety is a real issue. Anyone who says otherwise has not been paying attention. But there's a huge difference between all big AI players agreeing among themselves on how quickly a market should develop. This looks like an awful lot like competitors deciding who gets to compete, what they get to build, and when they may build it. The Big AI companies all look like good guys while simultaneously strangling their smaller competitors. To mere mortals, this may sound like an open-and-shut case. It's not. Antitrust law requires evidence of an agreement and actual harm to competition; executives making similar public comments is not enough. The plaintiffs will need considerably more than quotes about AI safety or responsible development to win. Besides, if they do win, so what? What recently looked like huge antitrust wins has had its teeth pulled when it came to actually punishing the likes of Google and its ad business, or its earlier "lose the case, win the settlement" with Google Search. Do you see the pattern here? Big AI has effectively argued that copyright law, open source licenses, and competition rules shouldn't slow them down. When creators object, they are told that training is fair use. When developers object, they are told that generated code is new code. When competitors object, they are told security requires the largest companies to coordinate. Funny how the answer always seems to leave Big AI with the data, the market, and the money, isn't it? The central issue isn't whether AI should be allowed to develop. It will develop. The issue is whether the companies building it should be allowed to treat everyone else’s work as a free raw-material supply, then use the resulting products to take away the creators’ traffic, revenue, and bargaining power. Unless we stop Big AI now from this land grab with GPUs, only a handful of trillionaires will really benefit from AI, with the rest of us becoming serfs in a 21st-century post-technology feudal system. ®
bc26475675090572: From Jamaluddin Aziz
Mara chairman Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki's call to end or restrict movies and dramas depicting bullying represents a familiar, knee-jerk reaction to deep-seated societal issues.

It is clear that while the anxiety surrounding youth violence in schools is entirely valid, the proposed censorship and blanket ban on creative narratives rest on an archaic understanding of how the media operates.
As media scholars, we have seen this script play out for over a century, and history has repeatedly proven that smashing the mirror does not cure the reflection.
To understand why this approach is fundamentally flawed, we must trace this anxiety back to the birth of media effects research in the early 20th century.
During the 1920s and 1930s, early theorists propagated what became known as the "Magic Bullet Theory" or the "Hypodermic Needle Theory".

This paradigm assumed that media messages were injected directly into a passive, helpless audience, immediately altering their behaviour and thoughts. It presumed that if a viewer saw violence on screen, they would inevitably replicate it on the streets.

By the 1940s, empirical research had thoroughly discredited this theory. Audiences are not a monolith, nor are they mindless vessels waiting to be programmed. Yet, the tradition of using the media as a convenient scapegoat for complex societal ills persists.

From comic books and rock music to video games and local cinema, authority figures have long favoured moral panics over structural analysis because blaming a screen is far easier than fixing a broken social fabric.

Crucially, the rapid evolution of media technology has completely transformed what it means to be an "audience". The very concept of "mass media" belonged to a bygone era of a one-to-many communication flow, a single broadcasting station transmitting to an uncritical mass. Today, that dynamic is dead.

The contemporary media landscape is highly decentralised and personalised. We no longer have passive consumers; we have "producers" who are individuals who simultaneously consume, critique, remix, and actively create content.
Modern audiences possess a sharp consciousness of their own individuality and exercise significant agency in how they interpret media.
Therefore, trying to eradicate bullying by banning a movie is a remarkably lazy policy response. It assumes a direct causal link that simply does not exist in a vacuum.

If the core fear is that a gullible audience will immediately mimic cinematic slang and adopt aggressive personas, we must look at the wider cultural landscape. Consider how the term "bossku" was enthusiastically adopted and chanted by political fans across the nation.

That phrase did not gain cultural dominance because of a movie script; it thrived because of real-world political dynamics, digital echo chambers, and active audience participation. Media does not dictate culture; it interacts with it.

To truly make sense of bullying and the bully, we must look beyond the screen. Banning stories about bullying only sanitises our media environment while leaving the actual victims unprotected in the real world.

We need to understand why bullying takes place, the psychological mechanisms behind peer pressure, and the systemic failures within our educational and familial institutions that allow aggression to go unchecked. To achieve this, we need rigorous data, not reactionary censorship.

I urge our relevant government agencies as well as the education; higher education; women, family and community development; and communications ministries to collaborate and offer substantial research grants dedicated to qualitative studies on youth deviance and bullying.
We must talk to the perpetrators, the victims, and the bystanders.

Only by conducting deep, qualitative research can we understand how bullies make sense of their own behaviour, how they rationalise their actions, and how subcultures form. Censorship is a temporary curtain; empirical understanding is the only real cure.
Let's stop blaming the filmmakers and start funding the solutions.
Jamaluddin Aziz is an associate professor in critical media studies at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia's Centre for Research in Media and Communication and an FMT reader.

773569ac081723f3: From Wan Agyl Wan Hassan
Malaysia does not lack road safety standards. We have engineering manuals, design guidelines, Road Safety Audits and experienced professionals across government.
But does every Malaysian receive the same minimum level of road-safety protection, regardless of who manages the road?

A motorcyclist does not become less vulnerable when moving from a federal road onto a state road. A parent taking a child to school should not need to know whether the road outside the school belongs to the public works department (JKR), the state or a local council.
An elderly person trying to reach a bus stop does not know which authority manages the crossing in front of them.
For road users, it is simply our road system.

Yet our roads are planned, designed and maintained by different levels of government. Federal roads, state roads, expressways and local authority roads have different functions, responsibilities and funding arrangements.

There are good reasons for these differences. An expressway should not be designed like a residential street. A rural road has different needs from a busy town centre. A kampung road cannot simply follow the same design as an urban arterial in Kuala Lumpur.
I'm not suggesting that every Malaysian road should look the same, but asking whether every road should meet an agreed minimum safety level.

Malaysia has already set the direction through the Malaysia Road Safety Plan 2022–2030, which targets a 50% reduction in road deaths by 2030 and identifies safer infrastructure as one of its priority areas.
The ambition is clear. The challenge is making sure the entire system helps deliver it.
When a serious crash happens, we question if the driver was speeding, whether the motorcyclist was careless or whether enforcement was adequate.
But they should not be the only questions.

Was the road designed for the speed vehicles actually travel? Could people cross safely? Were motorcyclists properly considered? Was the junction designed to reduce dangerous conflicts? Was the road properly maintained? Had development around the road changed how people were using it?
And when someone makes an ordinary human mistake, does the road environment help prevent that mistake from becoming a death or serious injury?
That is the thinking behind the Safe System approach. People will make mistakes. Our roads should be designed so that those mistakes do not routinely become fatal.

This is particularly important in Malaysia because motorcycles are part of everyday mobility. Any road-safety framework that does not consider motorcyclists from the onset will struggle to reflect the reality of our roads.
The same applies to pedestrians, children, older people, persons with disabilities, cyclists and people walking to and from public transport.
Road safety cannot therefore be measured only by how efficiently vehicles move. It must also consider how safely someone can ride to work, walk to school, cross a road or reach a bus stop.

We found that Malaysia's challenge is not the absence of technical guidance. We already have substantial engineering and planning standards. The question is whether their application across federal, state and local roads ultimately provides a common minimum level of protection.
We're not saying our existing system has failed. It is about strengthening what we already have.
JKR's own Road Safety Audit guidance recognises the importance of greater consistency in how safety audits are managed and implemented across different authorities.
Our road environments are also changing.

A road originally built mainly to move traffic may eventually be surrounded by houses, shops, schools, factories and bus stops. More people start walking and crossing. More vehicles enter and leave roadside premises. Motorcycle movements increase.
The road may carry the same classification, but the way people use it has changed. Our approach to safety must be able to respond to that change.
This is why Malaysia should begin discussing a common national road-safety floor.
The principle is simple. Different roads. Different functions. Different local contexts. One minimum level of safety.
A school zone should provide an agreed minimum level of protection whether it sits beside a federal, state or local road.

Pedestrian facilities should reflect the actual speed and risk of the road. Motorcycle safety should be considered in barriers, road surfaces, intersections and other conflict points. Road Safety Audits should identify serious risks and ensure they are properly addressed.
Roads should continue to be assessed as traffic, development and communities change.
This does not mean replacing existing JKR standards or taking decision-making away from states and local authorities. Neither should this become a federal exercise imposed on them.
A national safety floor must be developed together, recognising the responsibilities, expertise, local conditions and different implementation capacities of each level of government.

This matters because not every authority has the same resources. A large city council may have significant engineering capability. A smaller municipal or district council may face very different constraints.
If we agree on higher national expectations, we must also discuss technical support, capacity building, funding and realistic implementation.
That is why I do not believe we should begin with another directive, another manual or immediate legislation.
We should begin by getting everyone around the same table.

Malaysia should convene a National Roundtable on Safe Road and Street Standards, bringing together federal, state and local government, alongside our road engineers, planners, researchers, road-safety institutions and representatives of road users.
And it should start with one simple question: what minimum level of safety should no Malaysian road be allowed to fall below?
From there, we can examine what already works, where greater consistency is needed and where states and local authorities should retain flexibility.
We can also identify roads with the highest risks and progressively improve them.

Start with the areas where intervention can save the most lives. Test the approach across federal, state and local roads. Measure the results. Learn from them. Then determine what technical, regulatory or funding changes are actually necessary.
It should help us deliver the national road-safety ambition we have already committed to.
Malaysia already has capable institutions, engineers, planners and road-safety professionals. What we need now is to bring that expertise together around one common principle:
A Malaysian should not receive a different minimum level of road-safety protection simply because a road falls under a different jurisdiction.

Our roads may serve different purposes. They may be designed differently. They may be managed by different authorities. But the value of the person using them does not change at the jurisdictional boundary.
That is the conversation Malaysia should begin now. And getting federal, state and local government around the same table is the right place to start.
Wan Agyl Wan Hassan is the founder and senior adviser of MY Mobility Vision, a transport think tank.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
24b763f23e794b8a: The mood on the ground in Malaysia is heavy with a deep, suffocating weariness. People are simply tired
They are tired of politics and the power plays that have dragged focus, energy and resources away from building the economy and addressing the rising cost of living.

They are tired of watching the federal unity government navigate its own fragile choreography—with Umno Youth rattling sabres about realignments with PAS, whispers of possible early polls and convicted former prime minister Najib Razak’s conditional royal pardon which allows for house arrest.

Adding to the turbulence, the Negeri Sembilan political landscape appears to be spinning into administrative chaos. What began as a move by several traditional chieftains (undang) to remove the ruler has become more entangled and ugly with the involvement of the menteri besar and state executive council in a high-stakes power play.
The people are exhausted by a system where political survival and power are chased for their own sake, while ordinary families bear the brunt of rising costs and uneven development.

Compounding this instability is something even more dangerous: a profound crisis of public trust. Malaysians have grown deeply cynical, widely viewing politicians as power-hungry actors looking out primarily for themselves.
How do we break out of this exhausting loop? Perhaps the answer lies not in inventing new political spin, but in turning back the clock to timeless wisdom.

Global leaders occasionally lean on ancient texts to remind modern states of foundational statecraft. This was brought sharply into focus when reports emerged of India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi presenting Russian President Vladimir Putin with a Russian translation of the ancient Thirukkural on the sidelines of the recent BRICS summit in New Delhi.
Having read the text, I could understand Modi's choice of cultural diplomacy—taking a 2,000-year-old masterpiece on governance, ethics, and human conduct and placing it on the global stage.

Modi frequently quotes from the Thirukkural, as does our own Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. For instance, in tabling the 2024 federal budget in October 2023, Anwar noted that according to the Thirukkural, a good ruler is one who is capable of creating wealth, acquiring it, protecting it, and distributing it wisely for the welfare of the people.
In 2025, in talking about the burdens of the rising cost of living in Parliament, Anwar reminded Malaysians of the text's lesson that steadfastness of the heart is a core mark of human virtue.

Long before modern party politics and coalition arithmetic, the ancient Tamil text—composed by Tiruvalluvar—laid down a remarkably clear framework for governance. Its core principles offer an unsparing mirror for today’s politicians if they care to look.

Early icons of independent Malaysia understood this resonance. First prime minister Tunku Abdul Rahman heaped profuse praise upon the Thirukkural, as did national laureate Dr Ismail Hussein, who felt it held vital lessons for all of mankind.

Perhaps it’s time to introduce today’s politicians to this timeless wisdom, which transcends race, religion, and creed. We already possess distinguished Malay translations of the Tamil original, including works by Dr Ismail Hussein and Dr S Singaravelu, formerly of Universiti Malaya.

If our members of Parliament and state assemblymen genuinely imbibe these tenets, our public life could look entirely different, providing an ethical counterweight against systemic governance failures.
The Thirukkural rests on three essential pillars: aram (justice/virtue/righteousness), porul (material prosperity/politics/governance) and inbam (love/joy/human connection).

Aram deals with ethics, morality, and the leading of a balanced, honest life; porul focuses on the practicalities of governance, economics, and the social responsibilities of citizens and leaders; and inbam explores the nuances of intimacy, longing, and emotional connection.

The Thirukkural has many gems for both the ordinary citizen and rulers/leaders. For instance, it says good rulers/leaders are marked by courage, liberality, wisdom, energy, diligence and learning. They must also be easy of access and soft-spoken.

At the heart of the text with 1,330 couplets or Kural is a deep commitment to justice, the virtue that prevents resentment and division. Tiruvalluvar insists that true leaders must act with strict impartiality and safeguard the dignity of every single citizen.

In today's climate of fragile state-level realignments and casual ethnic grandstanding, this is more urgent than ever. Kural 317, for instance, states: "It is the highest wisdom not to cause pain to any living creature, at any time, in any degree, even in thought."

For our leaders, this is a practical warning against the abuse of power and divisive rhetoric that leaves communities feeling marginalised. Applying justice means defending an independent judiciary, maintaining fearless anti-corruption frameworks, and enacting policies rooted in equal opportunity rather than racial patronage.
Equally critical is the text’s emphasis on economic pragmatism and resource management, prioritising public welfare over elite accumulation.
For instance, Kural 385 says: "To acquire wealth, store it up, guard it, and distribute it wisely—these are the four distinct marks of an accomplished ruler (government)."

In practical terms, this means our leaders must stop treating national development projects as tools for cronyism or personal enrichment. Tax collected must be used for public benefit and every ringgit spent must be designed to uplift the people equitably.

The text places supreme importance on moral character and ethical duty. Leadership is not about bare political survival or relentless power plays; it is about steadfast integrity. As Kural 954 notes: “Even if wealth piled high is offered, those of good family will not do anything that lowers their honour.”
In a political culture scarred by broken promises, patronage politics, abuse of government resources and corruption, this is the missing link.

Ultimately, the Thirukkural is more than an ancient classic; it is a reality check for modern Malaysia. It reminds us that a nation’s true wealth is measured not by towering skyscrapers or quarterly GDP figures, but by the safety and dignity of its humblest citizen.
If our leaders have the courage to choose principled, people-centred governance over tactical survival, they - and we citizens - will find that Malaysia’s greatest days are still ahead.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
6663a1898a9696c8: India’s female labour force participation rate (LFPR) stands at 35%, which is well below that of peers like Bangladesh (42%) and the Philippines (50%).

Though it has risen substantially from 21% in 2017–18, a closer examination reveals that over 70% of the increase came from the agriculture and subsistence sectors, with significant levels of disguised employment.

Closing the female LFPR gap with the developed world is critical not only for advancing gender equality, but also for unlocking a substantial growth dividend. India could add between US$700 billion and US$1.4 trillion to its GDP.

But why do fewer women work in India to begin with? Much of the literature on this question has focussed on supply-side constraints, particularly societal norms, including the unequal distribution of unpaid care work, restrictions on mobility and education, weak legal protections, and practices such as child marriage.

The available evidence corroborates this. According to a UN Women technical brief, Indian women spent about 22% of their day on unpaid care work, compared to 6.4% of the day for men. Consequently, much of the policy response has focussed on increasing women’s share of existing jobs.
But this approach risks missing the mark, because even as several major constraints have eased in recent decades, women’s share of the nonfarm labour force has remained largely unchanged.

Education is also a commonly cited factor in Indian women’s low LFPR. But female enrollment rates now match or exceed male enrollment at every level. Similarly, child marriages have fallen by nearly half since 2005–06, and there has been a marked increase in women’s political participation.

Female voter turnout was around nine percentage points lower than male turnout in 1996, but by 2024, it had marginally surpassed male turnout. If norms alone were the binding constraint, there would have been a clearer shift by women into productive employment. That has not happened. The ratio of female to male nonfarm employment has increased by a meager 5% in the last two decades.

This disconnect suggests that the problem of low female LFPR also owes something to the lack of overall labour demand in the Indian economy. One way to illustrate this is through labour intensity: the amount of labour employed relative to the output produced.

India is considerably less labour-intensive than several of its peer economies. For example, Bangladesh, the Philippines, and Vietnam each employ roughly 40–50 workers to produce US$1 million of GDP, compared to only 35 workers in India. If India had Bangladesh’s labour intensity, its female LFPR (holding other variables constant) would be close to 50%.

India’s weak labour demand also shows up in the wage and unemployment data. Unemployment among young graduates aged 15–25 is around 40%, which suggests that the demand for labour is not high enough to offer young graduates sufficient wages to induce them to work.

The experience of Bangladesh’s ready-made garment (RMG) industry illustrates how labour demand can affect female LFPR. In 1983, the industry accounted for only 4% of Bangladesh’s total exports; by 2021, the share had increased to 81%, amounting to US$41 billion.

This labour-intensive export sector’s rapid expansion created millions of employment opportunities for women, who now account for over 60% of its employees. Without the expansion of the RMG industry, Bangladesh’s female LFPR would be close to 36%, similar to India’s.

So, what is keeping India’s labour demand so low? One important factor is the cost and complexity associated with employing labour. Around 15% of Indian firms identify labour regulations as a major constraint, compared with 3.4% in Bangladesh and 6.4% in the Philippines.
It is well known that cumbersome compliance requirements and restrictions on hiring and firing can increase the relative cost of employing workers, encouraging firms to substitute capital for labour.

India has also underperformed in precisely those sectors that have historically absorbed large numbers of lower-skilled workers. The value-added share of low-skilled, labour-intensive industries in India is around 16% of GDP, compared with approximately 20–26% in Vietnam, Indonesia, Bangladesh, and the Philippines.

India’s female LFPR could rise through two mutually reinforcing channels: faster GDP growth and higher employment growth. Faster GDP growth would boost overall demand for both capital and labour, and a more labour-intensive growth model would ensure that a larger share of that increased demand translates into jobs, thus creating more opportunities for men and women alike.

Three major reforms would help. First, India needs more flexible labour regulations. Recent reforms are a promising step forward, but further simplification of the labour code would reduce compliance burdens and lower the perceived risk associated with hiring workers.

Second, India must deliberately promote labour-intensive industries by alleviating constraints to their growth. That means addressing policy distortions, like input tariffs on man-made fibres, that make Indian labour-intensive manufacturing less competitive.
It also requires deeper access to global markets through more free-trade agreements, including the signing of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership.
Finally, India should substantially increase public investment in health and education, as these are large labour-intensive sectors that traditionally rely more on female labour.
Expanding the availability and quality of public services would create direct employment opportunities for women and improve the workforce’s long-term productivity and employability.

These reforms would lead to higher labour demand, which would increase India’s female LFPR. With more women in the workforce, social norms would evolve gradually, further boosting the female LFPR and creating a virtuous cycle.
Improving the female LFPR is not only a social imperative but also an economic necessity if India is serious about becoming viksit (developed) by the centennial of independence in 2047.
Shishir Gupta is a senior fellow at the Centre for Social and Economic Progress in New Delhi. Aalhya Sabharwal is a former research analyst at the Centre for Social and Economic Progress.

0d88d47b66c74bcd: Ringkasnya pada 20 Sept lalu Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir membatalkan pelantikan 10 Ahli Majlis Mesyuarat Negeri atau Exco berkuat kuasa serta-merta.
Empat hari kemudiannya, pembatalan itu diwartakan.

Oleh kerana Menteri Besar Ismail Lasim tidak mempersembahkan barisan exco yang baharu (sebagai ganti) seperti diperintah Yang Dipertuan Besar semasa membatalkan barisan yang terdahulu – Negeri Sembilan tidak ada seorang pun exco sehingga artikel ini ditulis.

Ertinya Ismail ketua kerajaan tanpa kerajaan. Umpama nakhoda kapal tanpa kelasi. Bolehkah nakhoda bersendirian membawa kapal belayar merentasi lautan sambil bertarung pelbagai cabaran - ditiup badai di atas laut bergelora?

Kalau tidak ada cabaran sekali pun, bolehkah kapal digerakkan in the first place? Tanpa anak kapal? Kalau serah senarai baru exco seperti yang diperintah, taklah begini jadinya. Assuming cadangan MB diperkenan baginda. Sekarang sampai bila begini?
Umum tahu keadaan ini ialah akibat krisis yang berlarutan. Persoalan paling penting sekarang – apa jalan ke hadapan?

Apabila Peguam Negara Dusuki Mokhtar mengulas krisis berkenaan berdasarkan bacaan perundangan dan perlembagaan ada pihak menyelar. Dengan keras memberitahu beliau jangan masuk campur urusan Negeri Sembilan.

Beberapa pakar undang-undang perlembagaan bagaimanapun berbeda pandangan. Bagi mereka adalah tidak wajar menuduh peguam negara campur tangan krisis dalaman Negeri Sembilan kerana beliau adalah penasihat undang undang tertinggi negara.
Saya setuju. Jika penasihat undang-undang tertinggi persekutuan tidak boleh ulas dan beri pandangan serta cadangan untuk menyelesaikan krisis yang bertambah parah, siapa yang boleh?
Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim juga diberi amaran oleh pihak yang mendakwa undang dan pemimpin adat Negeri Sembilan – jangan masuk campur.

Seperti yang saya tulis pada artikel terdahulu seorang pedana menteri wajib tahu apa yang sedang berlaku dan bagaimana ia dapat diatasi. Jika ketua kerajaan persekutuan tidak boleh melakukan apa-apa dan dituduh masuk campur, siapa yang boleh?

Apa pun semalam akhbar The Star menyiarkan laporan dengan tajuk "Anwar firm on not interfering in Negeri royal row". Perdana menteri dipetik berkata beliau tidak akan mencampuri urusan berkaitan kedudukan Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan tetapi berpendapat apa-apa pertikaian berhubung institusi raja mesti diatasi berdasarkan perlembangaan dan undang-undang.
Benar Negeri Sembilan ada perlembangaannya sendiri (seperti negeri-negeri lain di negara ini) dan adat pepatih yang unik seharusnya dihormati.
Namun ia tetap sebuah negeri dalam Malaysia sekali gus dirangkul Perlembagaan Persekutuan.

Saya mengaku sering bermain di minda adakah mungkin darurat diisytihar di Negeri Sembilan membolehkan federal goverment to run things at least sampai krisis diselesaikan? Atau kemungkinan PRN diadakan sekali lagi? Cuma letting my imagination to run wild.

Jumaat lalu saya dapati satu opinion piece siaran FMT yang amat menarik. Ia saranan dibuat oleh bekas hakim Hamid Sultan Abu Backer. Beliau mencadangkan isu Negeri Sembilan dibawa terus ke Mahkamah Persekutuan meski pun "pada masa ini satu-satunya laluan yang tersedia ialah semakan kehakiman”.

Bagaimanapun kata Hamid mekanisme itu menuntut semua pihak yang berlitigasi selesaikan terlebih dahulu proses rayuan yang panjang di Mahkamah Tinggi dan Mahkamah Rayuan sebelum sampai ke Mahkamah Persekutuan.
Maka semakan kehakiman dilihat tidak sesuai untuk krisis perlembangaan (which is what it is in Negeri Sembilan – a constitutional crisis) yang memerlukan tindakan segera.
“Untuk memintas keperlahanan sistematik ini, Mahkamah Persekutuan mesti menggunakan kuasa ‘suo motu’ agar suatu keputusan yang muktamad dapat diberikan secara pantas," kata Hamid.
Campur tangan 'suo motu' menurut beliau bertindak sebagai semakan berbentuk inquisitorial yang diaktifkan oleh jurisprudens sumpah atau Oath of Office jurisprudence.

Jujur saya akui ini kali pertama saya mendengar istilah 'suo moto'. Untuk tahu lebih lanjut sila baca penulisan Hamid di FMT, tiga hari lalu yang bertajuk '‘Suo motu’ cara lebih pantas selesaikan kebuntuan di Negeri Sembilan'.
Walaupun telah bersara, beliau tetap 'a learned judge'.
Akhir kalam, saya menegaskan krisis Negeri Sembilan semakin parah kerana pihak yang buat pertikaian sudah awal-awal made up their minds lalu tidak beri ruang untuk perbincangan lanjut.
Sambil mendakwa bertindak berpandu undang-undang dan perlembagaan.
Inilah digunakan untuk menidakkan hujah pihak lawan berdasarkan intepretasi sendiri.
Bak kata seorang kawan anak jati Nogori: "Nismilan: Tafsirlah undang-undang ikut selero dan puak masing masing."
Jelas si kawan sedih dan bosan krisis tak abih-abih.
Artikel ini ialah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
85bd5f12499167b7: From Moaz Nair
With over 5.4 million students packed into educational institutions nationwide, our schools are no longer just places of learning - they have become breeding grounds for systemic violence.

In 2024 alone, reported school bullying cases surged to a staggering 5,703. If that number does not shock you, the global reality should: Unicef confirms that at least one in three children aged 13 to 15 worldwide are subjected to the daily torment of bullying.

This crisis has escalated past name-calling and playground shoves into fatal territories. The starkest reminder of our collective failure is the horrific incident in Kuala Pilah, where a 16-year-old boy was detained under a murder investigation following the tragic death of a 14-year-old student at a school hostel - a nightmare stemming directly from suspected bullying.

Yet, we continue to foolishly shift the blame. Expecting teachers, headteachers, or university chancellors to police the psychological flaws of millions of students at every second of the day is a delusional abdication of responsibility. The problem does not originate in the classroom, and it cannot be solved there.
The mental ruin of the victim

Bullying is not a rite of passage; it is psychological warfare. The trauma inflicts deep, permanent scars, brainwashing victims into a misplaced sense of culpability where they blame themselves for the abuse they suffer. Trapped in a vicious cycle with no visible escape, these children face a soul-crushing sense of powerlessness.

This relentless terror triggers severe anxiety, extreme stress, and clinical depression. In the most devastating scenarios, it drives children even to suicide. Overwhelmed by the crushing weight of their tormentors, victims are effectively paralysed, stripped of the ability to stand up for themselves while the system looks on.
The dysfunctional family catalyst

If we want to stop this menace, we must stop ignoring where it starts: the home. Bullying tendencies do not materialise out of thin air; they are forged in broken domestic environments. A dysfunctional family life is a direct catalyst for hostility, impulsivity, and deep-seated anxiety. When a home environment fails to teach internal conflict resolution, it produces aggressive individuals who project their rage onto peers.

Too often, a bully is simply a product of severe parental neglect - a child throwing violent tantrums as a desperate, toxic cry for attention. Whether it stems from broken homes, domestic violence, or substance abuse, the pattern is identical.
The emotional neglect they experience breeds distorted self-esteem and a learned, hostile reflex. They grow up weaponising conflict because aggression is the only language they were taught at home.
The digital frontier: unchecked cyberbullying

The violence has expanded. Aggression has broken past the school gates and followed our children into their bedrooms through digital screens. Data from Ipsos reveals a horrifying reality: 23% of Malaysian parents report that their children have fallen victim to cyberbullying.

This is not harmless internet drama. Cyberbullying is a relentless, 24/7 campaign of terror that uses mobile phones, chat rooms, and social media platforms to systematically destroy a child. From vulgar threats to compromised pictures and cruel public comments, this continuous digital hostility constitutes severe psychological abuse. Like its physical counterpart, it erodes a child’s sanity and acts as a direct fast-track to attempted suicide.
Stop blaming schools, the defence starts at home

The bitter truth is that these deeply rooted behavioural pathologies start long before a student walks through a school gate. The absolute maximum an educational institution can offer is a reactive, band-aid counselling session for a student who is already broken. Schools cannot cure a rot that started in the living room.

If we want to permanently eliminate this epidemic, the family unit must take centre stage. Parents hold the ultimate power and the primary obligation. While they cannot police every peer group, they can no longer remain passive observers of their children's emotional wellbeing.

Parents must actively cultivate emotional resilience and iron-clad boundaries from day one. The only way to stop a bully - or to keep a child from becoming a target - is to build the defence where it matters most: at home.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

33fc23da63e90e0e: From Azam Mohd

Negeri Sembilan’s royal dispute is ultimately a test of constitutional method, not loyalty. Labels such as “derhaka” or “coup” may mobilise supporters, but they cannot substitute for proving jurisdiction, procedure, and evidence.

The state constitution gives the undangs a distinctive role. The Attorney-General’s Chambers acknowledged on Sept 17 that the chieftains possess power concerning a Yang Dipertuan Besar’s removal, but said Article 10 imposes mandatory grounds and procedures.

It found no evidence establishing the specified disqualification grounds and regarded the April 19 proclamation as invalid. The opposing Secretariat of the Undang Yang Empat subsequently maintained that preliminary and further inquiries occurred on March 5 and April 19.

What is clearer is what the executive cannot do. The AGC stated that the menteri besar and executive council possess no unilateral authority to terminate or vacate the ruler’s office. The Dewan Keadilan dan Undang likewise says Article XVI places questions of Malay custom, including appointment and removal, within the Dewan’s jurisdiction.

The menteri besar’s signature presents a narrower question. Umno’s published position says Article 10(2) makes the signature part of implementing an undang's decision, not the source of removal power. Yet whether a signature can validate an instrument depends first on satisfaction of the preceding constitutional requirements.
Ismail Lasim also alleged that an earlier signature was obtained under duress and lodged a police report. That allegation is evidence for investigation, not proof of criminal liability.

Judicial orders add another layer. On June 5, the Seremban High Court granted an ad interim injunction maintaining the existing composition of the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang and its secretary pending jurisdictional and justiciability questions or further order.

On July 8, the court granted leave for contempt proceedings against six individuals over an alleged breach; the Court of Appeal later stayed those contempt proceedings. Leave establishes a prima facie basis to proceed, not guilt.
Article XVI’s finality language concerning adat does not automatically erase judicial supervision over every procedural question.
Malaysian constitutionalism generally distinguishes the merits of an entrusted decision from whether the correct authority acted within constitutional limits.

Article 71 guarantees state constitutions and provides federal mechanisms in specified circumstances; Article 181 preserves rulers’ sovereignty subject to the Federal Constitution. Neither provision creates an ordinary shortcut for replacing Negeri Sembilan’s constitutional machinery. An emergency under Article 150 requires the constitutional conditions for a proclamation; controversy alone is insufficient.
Likewise, sedition, treason, offences against parliamentary democracy, arrest or disqualification require their own statutory elements and evidence. None follows automatically from disagreement.

The consequences nevertheless extend beyond Seremban. Melaka’s assembly was dissolved effective Sept 23, and its election must follow within 60 days. Barisan Nasional, Pakatan Harapan and Perikatan Nasional have incentives to frame Negeri Sembilan around loyalty, stability, and constitutional respect.

But there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the dispute will determine Melaka voting behaviour. Royal sentiment may influence some voters; household economics, candidates, turnout and coalition arrangements remain competing mechanisms.
For Umno and BN, the strategic danger is allowing legal ambiguity to become an identity test.
For PH and PN, exploiting unresolved proceedings as settled wrongdoing carries the same institutional risk.
The unity government’s interest should be narrower: preserve legal process, avoid executive improvisation, and ensure enforcement agencies act independently.

The evidence points to a dispute that remains legally conditional, not politically settled: Article 10 may empower the undang to remove the Yang Dipertuan Besar, but only if its mandatory grounds and procedures are satisfied; the menteri besar and executive council have no established unilateral power to do so; the validity of the April 19 proclamation remains contested; and any alleged breach of the High Court’s injunction is still for judicial determination.
Claims that criminal offences, disqualification, or federal intervention automatically follow are therefore premature, because each requires separate legal elements and proof.
That is why constitutional restraint, rather than partisan certainty, should define the response of every institution.

The responsible path is institutional restraint: preserve records, publish legally permissible reasons, obey subsisting court orders and let competent courts determine reviewable procedural questions while constitutionally designated adat bodies decide matters entrusted to them.
Negeri Sembilan does not need actors to manufacture a winner. It needs every institution to prove that constitutional authority still means authority exercised according to law.
Azam Mohd is an FMT reader.

ad169ad015f9c0e4: Our resident Microsoft-watcher Richard Speed last week wrote about his seven-hour odyssey bringing a Windows 11 box up to snuff with the latest patches. I’ll see you that struggle, Richard, and raise you my experience updating a 2022-vintage Samsung Galaxy A33 Android smartphone. I spent about a year using the A33 as my daily driver and while it always did a job, the midrange machine is far from the speediest of smartphones and therefore a little frustrating to use. When a great deal for a premium handset came along I splashed some cash and shelved the A33 as a spare, safe in the knowledge that Samsung has promised to support it with new security updates until 2027. I store the A33 in the Basket Full Of Old Tech I Should Probably Have Thrown Out But Kept Just In Case, which sits on the floor of my home office – a room that gets no direct sunlight but is small, warm, and dry. All through the mild-if-clammy winter here in The Register’s Sydney, Australia, eyrie, the phone insisted it had moisture in its USB-C port and refused to charge. Because it’s a budget model, topping it up with wireless power isn’t an option. Spring has since sprung, so when the mercury topped 30°C (86°F) last weekend I left the phone in a warm and breezy spot for an afternoon. The phantom moisture evaporated, and before long I had the phone charged and running. Within seconds it suggested installing an OS update from April 2025, followed by six more – each of which required manual consent for download and install. The A33’s sluggishness soon manifested as an overlapping mess of updates in progress and reboots to finish installation of the last update. Every few minutes, the phone wanted me to approve or schedule a new download, or log back in. The phone is not so important to me that I needed to get all the updates installed ASAP. Two days of occasional attention at mealtimes and bedtime earned me a slow, old, but functional backup phone. My experience led me to concur with Mr Speed’s excellent argument that vendors need to ship better software so they’re less reliant on updates – and improve the process of updating devices. For Samsung that means rolling up past updates into cumulative downloads so leaving a device offline for a few months requires one intervention to modernize a device. The Korean giant could also do well to detect when a handset needs multiple updates and then inform users that its Smart Switch desktop app makes it possible to install cumulative updates in one fell swoop. ®

6e8ae7ca7a0331e8: Britain’s Royal Air Force has gained some space cadets, in the form of No. III Space Effects Squadron, tasked with protecting critical satellites that the UK relies on for communications and navigation. Air Chief Marshal Sir Harvey Smyth announced the new unit at an inaugural UK Space Power Conference in London, saying it will safeguard the vital benefits that space gives to our armed forces, and be capable of denying those benefits to our adversaries. Smyth added that the RAF’s headquarters at High Wycombe transitioned to become Air and Space Command just a few weeks ago. According to the MoD, the existing No. I Space Operations Squadron and No. II Space Warning Squadron give the RAF the ability to watch and warn of threats in space, but the latest unit will have the ability to act against those threats. How, you might ask, given the UK has limited launch facilities and no anti-satellite missile systems, as far as we are aware? This will be accomplished using “advanced technology,” we are told, including electronic warfare, to “disrupt, degrade and deny hostile actions.” In fact, the government says the UK has formally ruled out destructive anti-satellite missile testing, and instead continues to work through the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space. That implies the use of ground-based jamming systems to disrupt or neutralize any nefarious foreign satellites. We asked the MoD for further details on what the space force’s capabilities consist of, exactly, but a spokesperson told us there is not much more that can be said as the information is classified. However, the MoD does say the squadron will support both offensive and defensive space operations and will expand over time as new capabilities enter service. The MoD states that satellites are critical for both national security and daily life, enabling intelligence gathering and missile warnings, while also providing telecoms and weather forecasts. The emergency services rely on satellite navigation systems for emergency responses, and energy networks use the same systems to organise power grids, making use of the precise time coding in such signals to synchronise operations. Last year, The Register reported that the MoD was working with the UK’s Space Agency on finding ways to protect orbiting satellites with technology that can spot when lasers are being used to try and dazzle them and disrupt communications. Four countries are known to have tested anti-satellite missiles; the US, Russia, China and India. The most recent incident was when Russia destroyed one of its own defunct orbiters in 2021, endangering the International Space Station. The ISS also had to conduct manoeuvres the same year to avoid space debris created by China blowing up one of its own satellites years earlier. In 2022, the United Nations passed a US-led resolution calling on countries to commit not to conduct any similar anti-satellite missile tests. That hasn’t stopped China, for one, looking at other ways of taking out orbital assets if it considers it necessary, looking at employing lasers and high-power microwaves to disable them. The US Space Force also claimed to have observed Chinese satellites practicing “dogfight” manoeuvres in orbit. ®
